messages.text: Ethereum issues tokens to ensure the security of the network. The guarantee that an issuance curve can provide on the inflation rate, is that its peak issuance rate caps the inflation rate. If the reward curve peaks at an issuance rate of 0.5%, then we guarantee a maximum inflation rate of 0.5% to users and holders of the ETH token. This seems like a reasonable cap on the issuance rate, and I therefore apply it for the reward curves presented in the practical endgame post.

my personal temporary conclusion post devcon debates has been:

- after 1+ year of issuance change discussions, there appears to be broader consensus that the current policy is economically & technically unsustainable long-term (even mostly acknowledged by folks from e.g. Lido)
- main reasons as mentioned above: (i) the network is structurally overpaying for security, (ii) undesirable network conditions in high staking regimes (leaving it to chance would be very 'un-ethereum')
- this lead me to believe that we're at a point where it's less about
we were to change but rather

(and the corresponding path towards that goal)
- biggest criticism however -as far as I understood it- remained: "we need more data" / modelling so that we make sure capped/lower issuance won't drive out solo/home staking

IMO, this is where broader Ethereum roadmap items come into play; namely shorter time-to-finality (technically necessitates smaller validator set), rainbow staking (unbundling of staking roles, i.e. 'what is a solostaker in the future?'), among others.
Put in other words: it will be much more difficult to arrive at shorter time to finality, i.e. 3-slot-finality (which many people in Ethereum/L2s want), without changing issuance. (think of Max_EB as a first stepping stone here btw)

A sidenote on driving out solo/home stakers: I think we have some compelling technical advancements on the horizon (beyond snarkifying everything) which will drive costs of running a node to ~0 and thus counter economies of scale of bigger operators (think of partially stateless clients like

announced yesterday which literally removes almost all costs of disk requirements)

I agree with Anthony that forming a narrative on changing issuance

has proven to be tricky, which is why I've personally shifted more towards embedding a potential monpol change into a broader, mainly technically based line of arguments cementing Ethereum's overall progress as a tech platform (and hence more indirectly about ETH value accrual)

edit:
-> single/three slot finality

I read your paper, and the two options you outlined are interesting. Please correct me if I’ve misunderstood anything, but here are my thoughts:

Practical Endgame (Lowering issuance to 0.5%) – I support reducing ETH issuance to strengthen its store-of-value appeal. As a home staker, my only ongoing cost is my internet connection, so I wouldn't stop staking due to lower yields. I’d gladly trade my current 3% yield for 0.5% if it drove ETH demand and price. However, at current burn rates 0.5% issuance is still inflationary which leaves uncertainty and a similar position to now.

Hard Endgame (Capping staking & imposing negative yields) – I agree with capping staking but dislike negative yields. Home staking isn’t very profitable, but it’s a way to support Ethereum while earning passive income. If I had to constantly monitor the cap to avoid losses, I’d likely just unstake altogether.

I'm not sure if this would work but this is an idea I had:
Cap Validators/ETH staked at 30% and have an issuance curve that reduces to zero when that threshold is reached. This ensures ETH remains consistently deflationary, increasing demand. Validators wouldn’t exit because:

-Their position is valuable (exiting means going to the back of the queue).
-They’d be holding a deflationary asset that benefits from ETH price appreciation.
-They’d still earn transaction fees, which should increase over time.

I believe decentralization is crucial, but I strongly disagree with this criticism and actually think the opposite is true.

As I mentioned before, I’m a solo staker, and my only ongoing cost is $80/month for my home internet —a cost I’d be paying anyway whether I stake or not. This means I can easily afford lower issuance, even if it went to zero.

On the other hand, centralized staking services like Lido rely on earning a commission from staking rewards. If issuance drops, their revenue may not cover their management fees and operating costs, making their model less sustainable. In contrast, solo stakers don’t have these extra overhead costs and are more likely to remain profitable.

text:
Not exactly. There are three different concepts here:

Issuance rate = issued tokens relative to supply: i=I/S, positive side of inflation
Max issuance rate = Only reached at peak of issuance curve
Issuance yield = what the stakers derive: y_i = I/D, where D is deposited tokens for staking. 

In these equations, issuance I is normally defined by these reward curves you have seen, from some specific equation relating to D. The current one being I = c*F*D**0.5, where c and F are just constants.

When I refer to a max issuance rate of 0.5%, I am discussing the rate when that I-curve peaks. It is used as a safety margin at a lower stake participation. At the current stake participation, i would fall down to around 0.35-0.4%, and then fall further if staking rises more. Setting the issuance rate to exactly 0 is problematic because the protocol will not be able to provide consensus incentives (a small reward for doing the right thing every epoch), less it takes out a fee from stakers. This topic was initially presented here:

A separate concept is the inflation rate s = i-b, where b is the burn rate consisting of the tokens the protocol burns each year, as a proportion of the circulation supply.

We can also note that stakers derive rewards also from MEV, and then usually describe the overall staking yield as y = y_i+y_v, where y_v is the yield from MEV.

Finally, we can now define the real yield, which a participant in the ecosystem derives by holding the ETH token. The equation is y_p = (1+y)/(1+s), which in accordance with previous stipulations can be separated into the specific components: 

y_p = (1+y_i+y_v)/(1+i-b)

Thus, we account both for the yield (which is 0 for non-stakers) and the inflation rate of the protocol.

I see my purchase of ETH as an investment, not part of a validator’s CAPEX cost. If I stopped validating today, I’d still hold my ETH. My  validator costs were $500-$1000 for equipment and $85/month for internet + power. That said, I understand your point about the high barrier to entry for new solo stakers.

I believe it’s important to focus on the present, so (A) retaining existing solo validators should take priority.

While improving MEV smoothing, timing games, and capital efficiency is valuable, I think the bigger issue is ETH’s long-term value. I doubt many Solo Stakers unstake to switch to Lido for this small difference in yield especially after they've already bought their equipment. I think there is a higher risk of people unstaking and converting their ETH to BTC than switching to Lido.

Since most of a solo staker’s investment is in ETH itself, the best way to retain them is to ensure ETH remains a strong store of value. High staking rewards mean nothing if ETH depreciates. This is a common goal for all ETH holders, not just stakers. The #1 requirement for ETH to be a good store of value is not inflating it away.

With blobs increasing, burn rates will decrease in the short term, leading to higher inflation. I think this issue is critical to address, and the only viable solution I can think of is reducing issuance.

While no staker wants lower rewards, I believe many would accept it if it created a deflationary ETH supply that increased demand for the asset. Existing validators have already covered their setup costs, so they can absorb lower issuance since operational costs are minimal.

In regards to (B) attracting new Solo Stakers with lower hardware cost and lower opex, I think its great for accessibility, but I question the quality and reliability of low-cost stakers. In my experience, people with more skin in the game tend to be more serious and committed. But that’s just my personal perspective.

I'm sorry but I don’t fully understand all the algebra. However, I do see why issuance can’t be reduced to zero due to consensus incentives. Would an alternative approach where issuance yield gradually reduces to 0.5% as staking nears 30% while capping the number of validators at this level address this while maintaining ETH’s deflationary model?

If issuance is reduced, I believe capping the number of validators provides a strong incentive for solo stakers to stay, as their validator position becomes more valuable. Additional benefits include:

-Rewards remain attractive as MEV and transaction fees are concentrated among fewer validators.
-Prevents large pools from expanding or dominating, improving decentralization.
-Keeps issuance low and predictable, reinforcing ETH’s store-of-value appeal.
-Supports Single Slot Finality (SSF) by reducing validator bloat.
-Avoids overpaying for security, ensuring efficient validator rewards.
-Encourages ETH liquidity, preventing excessive staking lock-up and maintaining economic flexibility.

Additionally, a queue with a 5-10 year periodic rotation mechanism could be introduced to cycle validators, or a system could be implemented to remove low-performing validators. This would help ensure the validator set remains efficient and competitive while maintaining security and decentralization.

text:
> All this leads to the death of solo stakers.

I think this illustrates a dead-end of the issuance debate quite fittingly:
"We need more data / modeling" on the one hand vs solo staking will remain economically rational because the cost of running a node will be ~0

As stated above, not looking at issuance changes in isolation and zooming out may represent a way out. Meaning asking the question: from a protocol perspective, what do we actually want from (solo) stakers as part of the future of staking while we optimize the network for higher throughput?

Do we still consider or even envision solo-stakers to be a realistic economic finality stop-gap? That would mean that we strive for at least >33% of stake being operated by them. For reference, today we have 5-10% of stake independently operated - arguably quite a stretch...

Or rather, do we want as many independent consensus participants as possible for highest possible censorship-resistance guarantees? This is what we benefit from the most given today's network topology: highly decorrelated attesting, at least partially viable local block building.

A powerful voice in finality vs guaranteeing CR are two distinct tasks, however. Instead of optimizing for a one-size-fits-all-staker, we probably should consider unbundling and redefining roles of what we used to refer to as solo-stakers. Rough consensus around a protocol future based on ZK and User 049S only adds to this.

One possible way to think about unbundled staking tasks which I find quite compelling could be 
i) FOCIL includers/attesters as

,
II) block builders/RPCs as

,
iii) sample providers/zk proof generators as

.

That is again why - IMO - issuance changes (i.e. how we incentivise potentially unbundled staking duties in the future) need to be embedded into a broader Ethereum roadmap context. They'll be one item among several (like rainbow staking, 3SF, APS, ...) in order to make the protocol long-term sustainable.

text:
I'd prefer different connotation :)

Solo-stakers are needed, always will be. In their role as attesters they're probably the last bulwark of credible neutrality Ethereum has.

Validators provide many different services by PoS design. Censorship-resistance is an important one, for example, today happening via local building. However, a vast majority of validators - solo-stakers included - have outsourced this duty, which leaves the network vulnerable to attacks. Inclusion lists are one possible network upgrade to change is. 

A somewhat similar line of reasoning applies to solo-stakers' weight in finality services as described above.

Meanwhile, the Ethereum community at the end of the day seeks for higher network throughput which is ultimately bottlenecked by bandwidth.

Note that unbundling staking roles in e.g. stateless/stateful clients and provers does explicitly not describe whether each task is fulfilled by solo operators or "pros"

. As an example, I'm optimistic that I can be a prover of a zkEVM block on my MacBook Pro in the future.  

As Ethereum continues to optimize for global scale, validators and thus solo-staker's tasks and duties shift, though their value in contributing to decentralisation remains unchanged.

Interestingly enough, the ability to scale Ethereum was only made possible by transitioning from PoW and out-of-protocol miners to PoS with in-protocol validators as consensus participants.
New era, differing roles. From a sustainable protocol perspective, incentives should and have change(d) accordingly.

Gm Gm. Many thoughts as you all know. Can we settle some standard definitions for real vs nominal inflation ;)?

I think a stratification of responsibilities (rainbow staking) is critical before we cut issuance. It’s hard to justify in the status quo when costs for solos are roughly equal to 0.8% APR on the position.

One of the difficulties of this debate is that the value definition of eth is not easily defined. Mass issuance cuts make a lot of sense if your value statement derives from “revenue” but if it’s“security/moneyeness” then the value to maximize is CR and the cost is outweighed by the benefits

messages.text:
Gm! - After reflecting a bit on this, I think we’re kind of stuck between a rock and a hard place with this.

Within this year, it’s likely we'll see all of these happening:
• MaxEB
• Staked ETFs
• Increased hardware requirements
• Increased blob revenue due to better economics of more blobs
• Increased block space revenue due to gas limit increases and better economics of L1 native DeFi, including stablecoin issuance

It’s extremely hard to predict the impact of these on staking participation - especially whether MaxEB by itself may be enough to fix the security concerns regarding the validator count.

I think it would be pretty bad to have an issuance curve adjustment hitting right before any of these things begin to play out, because then we’ll run into much worse narrative problems.

It’s probably best we either start to hit a "middle ground" or simply dismiss it until we have more data.

A middle ground would be to commit to the least invasive, absolute minimum change necessary from a security perspective.

Or we find a way to adjust the curve over time, so stakers are not hit "out of the blue" with a strong adjustment. We could even stretch this out over multiple years. This way, everyone knows what’s coming, but all the strong drivers for Ethereum revenue will have time to play out beforehand.

> 1. If you can change it once, proves that you can change it again

I'd say this meme depends on the perceived capriciousness and "granularity" of the proposed change. eip1559 was not accused of "well you can just change it again" because it was a totally new architecture and model with strong epistemological internals. If you're simply changing an inflation number and the diff is small, It invites skepticism over whether the new magic number is arbitrary and if there could be a newer arbitrary magic number in the future. However, if the change is a nontrivial overhaul to the economics, with great analysis/justification/telegraphing, then it can be credibly sold to the as the last needed change ever and not something capricious to happen again.

messages.text: I don't fully understand the implications of the roadmap proposals. I tend to believe that home stakers are more resilient to reductions in yield many of us seem to think. Home staking is resilient imo because it's seen as a civic duty - doing your part for the club good (for eth holders) which is ethereum neutrality - and also because home stakers, while not having as good economies of scale as professionals, tend to have lower costs due to not having to pay real estate rent/internet fees (as these are already purchased for your ordinary living), or staking operator fees. So I don't think home stakers are going to quit. Actually, I think the less attractive staking is for financial entities, the more it could become a sort of Marine corps for ethereum with a lot of pride.

> The proportion of active validators that are home stakers is not as important as the physical capability for the entire validator set to be agile and migrate to 100% home staking at a moment's notice should a disaster occur. 

I disagree. Home stakers are to keep the chain credibly neutral. Coinbase can run 2 million eth on 4 boxes in their employees houses if they need to post pectra, but if they refuse to use the focil gadget, ethereum is still centralised and decentralisation is over. If nodes are not independent it doesn't matter where they run.

messages.text:
You may have some home stakers who are very inelastic to returns but most of them will be OGs who have lots of ETH anyway, so it's not that they don't care about returns, just that they care less about the returns from validation as a % of total wealth. In terms of enfranchising new participants with low total networth and lower previous ETH bags, relying mostly on the values argument isn't really a winning move IMO.

In either case, the grim reality is that they most likely won't be a critical (in terms of stake weight) part of the network. They're important for CR and from an alignment / representation perspective. IMO higher stake rate generally means that in absolute terms the number of these participants goes up (even if the % share of the network may be less than in a low stake rate environment), which is good because it allows us to find ways for them to have outsized impact. Finding use cases (like FOCIL) where it's important to have as many honest participants in absolute terms IMO is the best way to advance network neutrality in the face of market dynamics.

> as long as it could rapidly jump to 100% of stake if a disaster occurred

What's your proposal for how that happens? Lets say in a mature capped environment, 50m staked, APR at 0.3%, min stake maybe $150k or multiples higher? 

> in case home staking becomes unexpectedly crucial due to a political development

I don't think we'll be able to undo Ethereum's soft-compromise if it happens. As an example, I don't think we would socially slash coinbase retail staked eth if they stop respecting FOCIL, or GHOST due to government pressure. This is something I've believed for a very long time

Open to being convinced otherwise, "Trust me we'll definitely be able to coordinate to burn all the normie's eth because coinbase started censorsing" is not a believable plan for me. Ethereum's not going to be compromised with a balancing attack on PoS by a bad actor, its just going to lose its censorship resistance through centralisation imo.

messages.text:
I think people really believe it'll be coordinated and some people really do intend on following through but don't appreciate that once that happens Ethereum's value is lost. A credibly neutral network that reaches mass adoption and then undergoes a non-neutral fork is not worth much except to the minority who chose to follow through with the UASF, and is thus worth much less in the aggregate. 

IMO the point is to make it such that "defection" by large staking blocs becomes untenable, and I think this is one of the things about high stake rate that is crucially missed — in order for it to happen it means that there is very high alignment between those who make the rules (validators) and those who allow them to do so (capital allocators). In a high stake rate scenario you have a large intersection between Holders : Users : Stakers, including (ideally) a high absolute number of participants who are both validators and capital allocators (staking on their own).

Sci fi:

Imagine that four US administrations from now a surprising coalition forms between America, Europe, and China with the goal of eradicating this pesky credibly neutral global economic hub. They make a coordinated strike on all centrally identifiable staking operations. The validator exit queue is months/years long. Inactivity leaks are high. In this scenario, we want the network to be physically capable of supporting an emergent cowboy league of ETH holders and freedom fighters that rapidly deploy a VPN home staking fleet to help the network finalize/run as normally as possible. I understand this story glosses over or errs on some of the technical details. But I think it's mostly correct to suggest that the network's capacity for home staking is more important than actual active levels of home staking.

messages.text:
I hear you on the idea/general direction, but i think an outage/dissappearance of the majority stake is not what we should worry about. That's more or less what's happened on holesky this month, we'd be fine. What we should worry about is US(DC) fork-choice rule. Imagine if instead the same coalition told the validators they could only attest to blocks that contained only transactions from/to attested addresses, outlawing whatever didn't agree to their demands? 
 
Something like FOCIL would allow a small minority of home/indie stakers to keep a larger group honest when it comes to including transactions, preserving ethereum's credible neutrality, but as barnabés tweet above points out, 6% home stakers == 63% censorship-resistant slots, and if we lose all cost-sensitive homestakers bar the ideological diehards, that's a far lower percent of CR than this FOCIL with today's chain diversity example even. Tornado is not mev-contentious, so it was still usable even when 90% were censoring blocks, but would uniswap and aave be okay? would *de*fi writ large survive? we need a large amount of home stakers, and we won't be able to get them retrospectively imo, so we better proactively accumulate them 🙂 

(Keep in mind they also help scale ethereum too! When we have PeerUser 049S, more home stakers will allow us to offer more User 049.)

messages.text:
Liking all these discussions! there are a few things there that I hope get a bit more clear as we release more notes on FOCIL in different contexts and futures of the staking. I do think we need nodes in the validator set that are not commercial entities, I think operator models with delegations and home nodes being part of larger protocols (lst's, dvt's) is meaningful and can get us far enough to have good FOCIL guarantees too.

> I think it's okay to have a small proportion of home stakers in the active validator set as long as it could rapidly jump to 100% of stake if a disaster occurred.
It's a good prompt to compare different models.
- The one that best fulfills this property long-term imo is Orbit, you can enter with low stake, you're online and engaged, but you're not going to be active very often, though you get a fair economic return that's not a priori worse than more active participants. But, making the Orbit model work seems like it's a lot of work.
- You could tell yourself "well as long as I have home stakers (so non-commercial nodes) who are maybe not solo stakers but part of larger protocols, and as long as they can protect/recover themselves from failures/capture of the larger protocol, I am happy enough". This opens the door for simpler mechanisms imo like capped validator set.
- Then the most hardcore version is "I don't actually care about having active home stakers in the set, as long as full nodes can quickly become staking nodes when need be". The issue is then that you lose the properties you get from FOCIL on the validator set. There is salvation in that you can do FOCIL outside of the validator set, à la Rainbow staking. But still, this might not be the validator set we want.

> When we have PeerUser 049S, more home stakers will allow us to offer more User 049.
that part is a bit iffy, it's more true in fullUser 049S (in peerUser 049S every node still has to download a fixed fraction of total data, doesn't matter if we have more nodes, we can't offer more data than any minimal node can verify)

messages.text: I'm not sure if any of you have experience with yield farming, but it often follows a pattern: when the token price is high, everyone unstakes to sell; when the price drops, people stake again. If token issuance is too high, whales tend to accumulate the majority of tokens, increasing sell pressure beyond demand. This can trigger a death spiral and lead to mass exits. Staking ETH is starting to feel a lot like yield farming on SushiSwap. I really hope you can lower the issuance soon to prevent this from happening.

On the question of narrative, I wonder if all of this would be a lot more palatable if presented not as an issuance cut (because the new curve keeps issuance at current staking levels the same) but fixing the faulty parts of the curve (which are further out along the participation rate than we are at today).

Then the only way you could object to the change is if you actually believe we should be incentivising very high staking ratios, which is the debate we  should actually be having, rather than all the objections that "cutting issuance has effects X or Y on the validator set".

Because of course as staking participation increases, real issuance tends to zero anyway. All you are doing by changing the curve is ensuring that happens at a point where raw ETH is still a thing.

I think this could/should also be discussed. It's true if:
- ETH is the only asset in the world, and
- all else stays equal (i.e. that the demand for ETH as an asset, e.g. expressed via its price, doesn't fluctuate).

Basically, I disagree that real yield is zero because most costs are denominated (both for actors in the current economic system and especially costs related to operating nodes and validators) in fiat, not ETH. Therefore even if all ETH holders are receiving yield as a part of participating in the ecosystem and thus the issuance is essentially zero across all of them, because ETH can appreciate contra other assets that are a part of the digital economy (and especially the assets required for infra operations), real yield can still be positive.

messages.text:
Engineering lift for updating issuance is low. There are some nuances, e.g. Anders' work focuses on tampered curves that never quite go to 0 - these are simple parameter adjustments, very little engineering / testing work. Also some variants of the other proposed chages, to the extent they keep some minimum tail issuance.

Most other proposals (by Caspar & me, but also the newer one by Justin) instead include a point at which issuance would stop. Those would require some more work, because they need to change the overall mechanism a bit so that there is still a participation incentive in the range of 0 issuance (even if we don't expect to ever get there in practice, chain must obv still work there). Still not a huge lift, but some significant work.

Still not a huge lift, but some significant work.

Much more relevant factor is social consensus though. Caspar and I initially hoped to make a relatively short term adjustment, because it looked like ther was a lot of staking inflow pressure.

But obviously our work was poorly received, so this made me personally update towards really taking our time exploring this topic conclusively, building social consensus around what to do, and only then making a change.

Downside is of course that we might in the meantime move into a meaningfully different staking regime (say >50% staked).

To elaborate a bit more: my proposal is not for actual issuance to move to 1% per year, but to have an in-protocol rule that makes it impossible to go beyond that, effectively bounding the design space. This means that in practice the change would be a “no op”, but we’d have an in-protocol guaranteed bound. 

My rationale is that I’m skeptical we can credibly claim whatever issuance change we make next will truly be the last one, but fairly confident we can claim to never exceed 1%.

The biggest downside is that the code changes are non trivial, for what is basically a “meme feature” 😅

as a home staker, i would say that my decision to stake is far more influenced by the ease of setup, maintenance, and troubleshooting than actual yield. i would likely still stake under 1% because the other decision palatable to my risk tolerance is to just hold that eth in a wallet. i don’t think we should think of ETH staking as competitive to defi yields - i think we should think of it as competitive to ETH just sitting in a wallet. i wish it *were* a competitor to defi yields, but the fact that larger providers are pressured to provide yield means that home stakers just can’t compete with them when staking yields are high. 

if yields are sub 1% and there’s a viable defi strategy that offers a much higher yield, why wouldn’t providers offer that strategy rather than staking in the long term? yes, they view staking as very low risk, but i do think that as defi matures, they’ll be able to better defend and assess low-risk strategies that’ll pull them away from staking

my primary concern as a home staker is not my nominal yield (though it is definitely secondary), but the sustainability of the core protocol. i think easing the home staking experience would have a far bigger impact than raising my yield by some basis points

messages.text:
This isn’t about "pumping the price" in the short term—it’s about ETH’s long-term competitiveness, particularly as a store of value. The ETH/BTC ratio is not the sole justification, but it’s a valid signal reflecting market confidence in ETH’s fundamentals over time.

ETH needs to be competitive against BTC as a store of value if we want it to remain attractive to long-term holders, institutional capital, and participants in the staking ecosystem. Tokenomics are central to that.

Since the Merge, the introduction of blobs has significantly reduced the burn rate, and from what I understand, the plan is to continue scaling blob capacity for the next several years. That means the burn mechanism will remain weak for the foreseeable future, resulting in higher net inflation.

If the burn is no longer an effective check on supply growth, the only viable alternative to maintain ETH’s monetary integrity is to reduce issuance—especially as the staking set grows. Aligning incentives by adjusting rewards isn’t just about short-term economics—it’s about preserving ETH’s credibility and long-term value proposition

It's also an awkward part of the strategy where right now rate of increase in capacity (via L2s) is outpacing increase rate of growth in network demand (especially at L1, but even at L2 level where that demand translates into less value for the L1), which has had negative implications on market's "assessment" of ETH as an asset (for a variety of reasons: it's hard to assess and understand Ethereum as a synthesis of L1s and L2s, not only because of unclear direct value accrual but also because of L2 tokens, etc), because of the rewind on the ultrasound money meme, because ETH is a pretty good asset to pressure right now if you have large bags, long time horizons, and asymmetric information about possible growth in the future, etc).

All of this aggregates into "price rly bad" and that make us want to react to that, which is for sure reasonable. I just worry immensely about trying to treat this with deep structural changes vs trying to treat largely market-related symptoms.

I agree with hasu here. Been pretty quiet in here as I work on my essay but I largely argue that the issuance debate is missing the forest for the trees - what value are we maximizing for? I tend to agree with hasu that we must maximize value creation. What underpins value creation on Ethereum? I argue credible neutrality. Thus, the issuance debate is a balancing act between maximizing credible neutrality based value creation and issuance. 

For example, if we believe that Ethereum is not like a dcf stock a la Solana, we would make the wrong decisions to maximize values like them. Ex: extreme MEV in a hypothetical state can drive up “REV” but cause centralization of the node set. In DCF land this is great, but if the value of ethereum is based on value created, then this would be bad! 

Largely I think of the burn as a supply control like interest rates at the fed but automated. REV just like the FFR doesn’t change the value of an economy but it does set a multiplier. The value of Ethereum is not based on fees.

Imagine 100% ETH is staked, and almost everyone holds it in the form of an LST. That LST may be designed as representing a share of the underlying ETH _including_ ongoing rewards. So the LST's value as a proportion of the total ETH supply remains constant. LST holders don't receive any income (so no tax), but neither are they diluted. 

Now imagine I'm the last sucker running as a solo staker. My 32 ETH is being diluted by issuance, but this is compensated by the rewards I receive. Except those rewards are taxed as income! So overall I get diluted and the rewards which would compensate for that dilution get taxed. So I am at a massive disadvantage compared to the LST holders. Of course I won't continue as a solo staker under such circumstances.

my purpose here really isn’t to pick on you but to illustrate the failure of the current staking experience / economics / structure. you’re extremely knowledgeable, very capable, and a staunch advocate of home staking but you yourself don’t run a validator (or didn’t when i spoke to you six-ish months ago) and *do* hold LSTs. the current situation isn’t good for the protocol or home stakers. its strongest period of onboarding solo stakers was at genesis when the narrative was the need for them to bootstrap the network

even if home stakers were served by a higher issuance regime (which i contend), the network isn’t there to serve home stakers and i think we get derailed when we talk about us as if we’re some protected group. if the current conditions can’t get people like you to stake, there is active structural failure happening and i don’t like talking about the

as if it’s what we have to resign ourselves to. when >50% of ETH has an active interest in fighting any issuance changes, you can bet the bikeshedding and filibustering will be much greater than it is at 28%. and i think we can be much more creative as an industry than essentially enshrining the ‘lesser evil’

and i still don’t understand why coinbase or any centralized entities would continue to throw infra and resources at 0.1% when they can pivot to other forms of yield, especially when staking risks become increasingly apparent by things like the recent holešky situation - the “risk-free” rate is suddenly understood as not so risk-free

text: My 2 cents as a solo staker and a die hard supporter. I’d continue to solo stake no matter how low the APY/issuance goes as long as it remains profitable. Simply to support the network, and because like

said many of us that are used to solo staking will just view it as an alternative to ETH sitting in cold storage. So any yield (as long as it’s profitable enough to cover opex) is better than nothing.

I think it’s safe to assume that:
1. Most solo stakers fall into that category.

2. Only the most hardcore supporters/hobbyists would even bother trying to solo stake. I doubt there are many newcomers eager to learn how to solo stake for a meager 3%. Won’t change if it goes up to 5% or down to 1% etc. Staking APY + mev just continually trending lower anyway, if anyone still wants to inconvenience themselves to learn it’s probably for idealogical reasons. 

IMO as long as we make solo staking accessible to those that are interested (via reasonable hardware/bandwidth reqs) then I don’t think we have to worry about the level of issuance affecting solo stakers’ decision to participate.

Re issuance I think it’s more important to just find an optimal strategy so we don’t  ever end up in scenarios like:

1. Way too much ETH staked for suboptimal reasons (like Tezos or other vapor chains where 80%+ of supply just staked)

2. ETH losing its monetary premium in defi in the above scenario and entire ecosystem moves towards a few LSTs as the primary asset etc.

> I’d continue to solo stake no matter how low the APY/issuance goes as long as it remains profitable

Do you fancy estimating your annual costs for those that don't solo stake here? 🙂  And would you delegate stake versus solo staking if it got too costly or would you refuse to delegate stake entirely? 

 e.g. $1000 machine, 4 year lifetime, $250 per year on hardware. Maybe 55 watts of power, so call it $110 on electricity @23c per kwh. Some contribution to your internet bill (say 10% of $40/mo) so another $50. $0 on labour... 

At $2k eth, 1 validator, a 0.8% apr, that's $512 per year versus $410 in costs before labour, (vs $50 in costs to delegate stake).  At 3.5% APR your costs are 18% of what you make vs the 10% delegation costs. What does 'profitable' mean to you, flat out just making more than zero dollars after costs? or should solo staking be in the same ballpark as the costs of delegation for you to keep doing it?

Hey Oisin! Yea I’d estimate my annual costs to be around $500.

I realized I might not be a  good benchmark since I’m running multiple validators so it’s easier to be profitable. Though it’s just anecdotal, I feel like almost every solo staker I know is doing the same since they were early supporters from 2017-2020. I think I only know 1 solo staker actually running just 1 validator (maybe someone can check the stakecat list to see what % are just running 1, kind of curious now)

In your example of 1 validator at 2k ETH and 0.8%. If I only had 1 validator I’d still solo stake because at that point we’re talking about an insignificant amount of $ relative to the stake involved. Netting $100 solo staking after costs vs $460 to delegate stake on a $64K balance. I’d still rather solo stake since I’d view forgoing that $360 as the small cost of supporting the network + being able to self custody.

It would probably take some weird scenario where delegating stake yields a significantly higher amount in absolute dollar amounts for me to reconsider solo staking. 

I.e. if solo staking 1M worth of Eth yielded 20K vs delegating 1M on a trustworthy CEX like kraken/CB that managed to yield 40K.

The latter option would be pretty tempting. But if it was 20k vs 25k the difference wouldn’t be enough for me to reconsider. If that makes any sense.

Even at $500 per year, that’s less than $10 a week. Compared to your 32 ETH investment, it’s a small cost — but in return, you get peace of mind through self-custody and the pride of actively contributing to the security of the Ethereum network.

Ask your Rocket Pool validators this: would they rather earn slightly fewer rewards on an asset that’s consistently deflationary, or make an extra $3 a week on electricity savings?

And beyond that, ask the broader ETH community: would you prefer to hold an asset that is deflationary or one that’s inflationary?

To me, the answers are pretty clear.

So zero issuance at 50% staked or 2% issuance at 100% staked are in one sense equivalent (no one is actually earning anything) except that in the 100% case:
1. we no longer have any pristine ETH (it's all intermediated through a staking provider)
2. If there were any solo stakers left they would be both diluted and taxed - so their stake would be eroded.

Bear in mind that the implications for (2) in particular scale with the price of ETH! My electricity costs are negligible and will not significantly change. But if ETH becomes more valuable in the 100% case, my costs go up.

> no one is actually earning anything

I think you misunderstand when we use the term Home staker vs Solo staker. 

Your rationale only applies if you assume everyone runs their own validator, but in practice maybe 6% of the network does, everything else is delegated, either to CEXs/LSTs on one end of the spectrum, or to minipool operators and squad stakers on the other. The vast, vast majority of nodes on the network earn nominal * commission, not the real rate, unless you have a proposal on how to prevent this, delegation will continue, whether inside or outside the core protocol. If you re-look at the economics of the machines that constitute the network in this lens, you can see that the delegatees make very different amounts in a capped vs uncapped world, and if you do (nominal*commission)-cost, you can see that only one of these outcomes can support node operation with call it 5 figures USD of delegated eth, the other needs maybe 8/9 figures USD delegated depening on your assumption of equilbrium APR under croissant and equilibrium commission.

I just listened in on the research call, and from what I understand, achieving single-slot finality requires reducing the size of the validator set. The favoured approach seems to involve phasing out low-stake solo stakers in favour of higher-stake home operators who receive delegated stake from protocols like Rocketpool, Lido, and Obol.

This raises a question, how independent can a home operator truly be if they rely on these protocols for the stake that enables them to operate? Doesn’t that, in effect, give the protocols significant control over the operators?

Additionally, does this effectively shut down the issuance reduction discussion? Since these protocols earn commissions, and higher rewards mean higher profits, wouldn’t they naturally resist any move to reduce issuance?

messages.text:
Utility vs. Scarcity
Steel is one of the most useful materials on earth. It’s everywhere in buildings, bridges, cars, tools. It literally holds up our civilization. But despite its enormous utility, steel is cheap. Why? Because it’s abundant. It’s easy to produce, and more of it can always be made.

Gold, in contrast, doesn’t hold up bridges or build cities. It’s not particularly “useful” in everyday life. Yet gold is expensive because it’s scarce. Its limited supply makes it valuable. People and countries store gold - not steel as a form of wealth.

This is the core tension between Ethereum and Bitcoin.

Ethereum is like steel. It’s powerful, flexible, and foundational for smart contracts, DeFi, NFTs, and decentralized applications. Its utility is undeniable. But despite the Merge and its move to Proof of Stake, Ethereum's supply dynamics are still relatively flexible. The issuance policy is complex and can change based on network decisions, gas fee burn rates, and validator incentives. While Ethereum sometimes becomes deflationary during high usage, it's not consistently so.

Bitcoin is like gold. Its supply is capped at 21 million. The rules are hard-coded and predictable. That scarcity gives Bitcoin its narrative as digital gold and that narrative has traction, especially with long-term investors, institutions and countries.

For Ethereum to compete with Bitcoin as a store of value, not just as a utility chain it needs to lean harder into scarcity. That means making its issuance policy more predictable, transparent, and consistently deflationary which is what the croissant proposal does. Utility alone doesn’t preserve wealth - scarcity does.

Until ETH becomes truly scarce, it will continue to lose value to BTC and our inaction is like watching a car crash in slow motion.

messages.text:
Gold isn't really that scarce. There are things that are a lot scarcer than gold that are worth much less because there's no memetics behind their usefulness as an SoV. It's somewhat scarce but it's more-so that its scarcity became a meme. You will never out-meme bitcoin in this, because it's the only thing bitcoin does: it's a hardened digital store of value because of a shared memetic belief that it functions as a good store of value plus some additional factors (eg it was early, similar to how gold was early as a commonly understood SoV, ironically in part because it was relatively scarce but not scarce enough where it could only be found in 1 geographic region etc). 

If Ethereum tries to outcompete with bitcoin in that arena it will lose. Ether is that's something that's meant to be used — it's the lifeblood of the network. When you attempt to use scarcity as the main momentum for price action of an asset (like bitcoin) what you do is push people to NOT use it, because it's silly to use something that you think will increase in value.

Utility is good but realistically institutions don't buy millions of dollars in ETH to use it for gas. Demand comes from people wanting to invest in the asset and that's why billions of dollars flows into BTC.

I see ETH not just as a utility token for applications, but as the foundation for a future global financial system. Imagine every country issuing its own digital currency stablecoins/CBDCs all settling on Ethereum. People would use local stablecoins for everyday transactions, then convert back to ETH as a store of value, especially as their national currencies inflate. In this model, ETH becomes the neutral global reserve asset anchoring a new digital economy.

As the world becomes increasingly multipolar, I believe the US dollar will eventually lose its position as the global reserve currency and that creates a void. While Bitcoin currently leads as a digital store of value, I believe ETH is far more suitable for this role. You don’t want to just be the platform the world economy runs on - it’s better to be the reserve asset it stores value in.

But for ETH to step into that role, it needs more than utility - it needs trust. That means a clear, predictable, and ideally deflationary issuance policy. Sovereign wealth funds and central banks won’t hold an asset with flexible or uncertain monetary rules. They need stability, scarcity, and long-term credibility.

I think what’s being pointed out is that we want ETH to serve as collateral and incentive for validators but also be a medium of exchange, not to be supplanted by USDC. 

We can have a fractured ETH ecosystem (like the status quo) with numerous LSTs and naked ETH that’s slowly losing share, or we can unify the assets through a partial enshrinement and get the best of both worlds. The current system has too much value being spent on liquidity that’s unnecessary. It also limits some of the velocity of ETH as a result of fragmentation. 

A partial enshrined world could help unify liquidity and make the velocity grow through universal standards. 

I’m not sold that emissions correlate strongly with velocity however. Most LSTs are held passively. There’s a loose sense in which this correlation  happens through rate arbs. If the borrow rate on lending markets is below LST Apr, there is a native DeFi trade to be had but I would argue these looped staking strategies lower velocity potential. Sitting in a looped staked position is not very meaningfully different than just a staked position. In fact, it’s worse since the lst is more easily used for other activities than a DeFi position. 

Real velocity imo is ETH being traded or used within dApps that derive a yield from outside of staking (DEXs, bonds, direct transfers, paying fees, irl payments). This is the type of active demand we need to generate for ETH. Issuance relates to this insofar as it impacts the cohesion of the ETH economy.

messages.text:
I think you nailed it on the dual nature of the token.

In theory, a world where everyone transacts in ETH sounds ideal but in reality, it's unlikely. Even with the USD as the global reserve currency, countries still rely on their own currencies for domestic transactions, driven by local economic policies and regulations. Crypto adoption won’t change this, nations will continue to favor local tokens for stability and sovereignty. 

I see your point with the voting analogy, but I don’t think community voting should be solely based on token balance. It risks favoring whales over long-term contributors but in the end thats for the local government to decide.

Fortunately Ethereum is built for this. With its Layer 2 ecosystems, communities, governments, and applications can create their own tokens and set their own rules, while relying on Ethereum as the settlement and security layer.

Although Ethereum’s monetary policy seems well defined to us, the market signals otherwise. Institutions, nations, and even ETH holders are migrating to Bitcoin, drawn to its clear and predictable monetary policy. Many of us want to hold the asset most likely to become the global reserve. Platforms can be replaced; the reserve asset cannot. Ethereum needs to compete with Bitcoin on this front before it’s too late. If Bitcoin wins, it becomes the dominant store of value and will be used in wrapped form across all chains.

The only lever Ethereum can control is issuance. Burn rates are unpredictable due to variable usage and ongoing upgrades. We need a clear, minimal issuance policy that preserves wealth without requiring staking to do so.

messages.text:
Concerning issuance policy I will say the following. 

Lower issuance benefits Ethereum in two key ways:

1. It increases welfare by reducing the costs users are compelled to incur.
2. It strengthens resilience and trustlessness.

Current CR research and new consensus requirements tip the balance further in favor of these benefits.

A. We know that the validator incentives will need to be adapted for SSF.
B. We know that FOCIL will alter the role of stakers.

Once the future staking landscape is defined, a congruent reduction in issuance should be determined, under renewed debate.

messages.text:
mev burn removes (part of) the direct payment of mev to the validators. so instead of mev being part of the cash flows accruing to stakers, it’s internalised more directly by holders instead. this lowers naturally the supply of stake curve, understood as the quantity of ETH willing to be staked at some given yield. so releases pressure on these debates and also removes (again, maybe only partially depending on the designs) a key source of reward variability

in my view there’s two broad classes of mev burn mechanisms:
- direct validator constraint: the validator is initially given the block proposing rights, but an open auction enforced by attesters ensures that the validator picks one of the top bids. think ePBS + some type of consensus over the bids received that surface the value to be burned
- APS-type proposals: the block proposing rights are more directly allocated to a distinct class of nodes than validators, which receive these rights from some mechanism. The mechanism can then burn some of the payments received to bid in the allocation. The chosen block proposer then recoups their cost by extracting MEV from the block they propose

text:
Here are my point of view (ex web2 mar-tech entrepreneur & ex large cap CMO/VP Marketing, now ETH investor and a nobody in the community)
I’m far from as technical as most of you in here, so giving my input limited to marketing and economics (value). Will be a bit long will cover also the most recent disuccsions about issuance vs. price.

text.text: In the Issuance/burn discussions, we prioritize two things: value of Ether & chain security

text:
I believe we maxemize this by following this priotization:
 1. Minimal Viable Issuance (issue as few ETH as possible while keeping maximum security and decentralization)
 2. Maximize adoption (Indirectly burn ETH & holdings ETH to use it)
 3. Maximize ETH burn (min fees etc without hurting #2, in this context 2x blobs or 2x gas limit = 2x min blob fee or 2x gas fees, we don’t need to increase min. wei, we can assume utilization because of #2 is higher than #3 and everything else is outside this scope)

⁃ Maximum, Minimim are tiers, it’s not the same things as “Maximize and Minimize”, which is a strive towards 100% or 0%.
 ⁃ So, Maximum security is NOT as much as possible, it’s a tier, like S-tier, “if we are here, we’re at the highest level”
 ⁃ Once S-tier security from validator rewards is defined, we can adjust issuance based on +-X% of validators and +-Y% of price. (To my understanding Ethereum is aware of amount of validators but not the ETH/FIAT price, therefore adjustments can and should be made by humans to this as the FIAT value of ETH moves to different levels and the levels are a function of amount of validators)
 ⁃ Maximize adoption is on the other hand as much as possible. The key here is “adoption value” giving out all ETH reserves as grants to maximize short turn and another fork of a DEX is not the same “adoption value” as a small test project from a large financial institution.

⁃ SHORT: Ether has, and will always strive for a Minimal Viable Issuance with maximal security.
 ⁃ LONG:   Ether has, and will always strive for a Minimal Viable Issuance with maximal security. Measurements are taken constantly in every upgrade to achieve this goal and always push the boundaries of being an as good of store of value possible
 ⁃ SHORT: Ethereum has the most secure blocks and Ethereum Layers, people & institutions are paying for this.
 ⁃ LONG:   Ethereum has the most secure blocks and Ethereum Layers, people & institutions are paying for this, the value accrual from this goes towards higher security and scarcity of Ether.
 ⁃ Ethereum achieves higher security with lower issuance compared to other blockchains with it’s base layer and higher throughput with lower fees than other blockchains by scaling with “Ethereum Layers” (I made up “Ethereum Layers” here… mixing L2s, rollups, appchains, sidechains, blobs etc is no way to communicate externally, the phrase “Network Extensions” is better for external communication IMO but Ethereum Layers will partially easy the debate of "L2s aren't Ethereum, Ethereum doesn't scale etc.”)

⁃ If we say Ethereum has Minimum Viable Issuance as a goal, not changing the code would actually change the more than changing the vision.
 ⁃ If Bitcoin can have 0.8% with PoW, ETH must have less than that with PoS - If we don’t believe this, isn’t our definition of S-tier (maximum security is probably wrong)
 ⁃ The scarcity of Ether is unique and must be communicated, communicating/marketing less supply creates demand => increase usage => creates less supply …and so on
 ⁃ There’s nothing wrong of saying “prioritize the value of Ether”, an increase of the value of Ether will help reduce the issuance of Ether making it a more efficient asset (this can be said without being greedy ETH price maxi)

⁃ Burn them, Staking rewards should be smooth and predicable, staking should not be a lottery (smoothing pools in BTC decrease decentraliztion)
 ⁃ If rewards for validators aren't enough the issuance curve should be increased
 ⁃ Users should never need to understand or worry about MEV. 
 ⁃ Wallets should solve UX for tips, they should exist, but should be burned
& ETH price

⁃ All issuance will eventually change hands, some today, some in a year, some in a decade, so over time all issuance will become sell pressure
 ⁃ Issuance is not sold evenly, this reduces price stability, adding risk for investors, which harms the goal of increasing to value of Ether
 ⁃ I’ve scrolled this chat and seen price discussions on buyback etc, in a demand/supply economic, we can only control supply and create demand with: stable rules (reduce risk), narrative (lowest issuance). A buyback is a shock and therefore a pump in price.
 ⁃ Lower issuance drives some demand - For people who care about issuance lower risk of takers during yield in bear markets etc
 ⁃ Lower issuance reduces some demand - For people who care about staking yield, these people as long as they hold vill become ambassadors (pump my bags) so there’s temporarily also a benefit of having them hold instead of burning it. And oUser 079 a constant feed of “temporarily” creates something like a permanent state.
 ⁃ I believe (but just guessing oUser 079) that _IF_ communicated/marketed correctly, the pros will outweigh the cons when lowering issuance creating the positive loop explained above.
 ⁃ There’s no arguing that demand drives price much more than supply can increase it. But at least with supply we can add a multiplier to the ratio between them. So make demand 10X vs 5X supply increase, but profit taking will always be the big number, which we only can control by improving the asset to a degree that they always push the goal post of profit taking to the future.

Good/best way to prevent pools/CEXes from taking over all stake if there's a validator cap and not profitable. Perhaps some proving with ZK is possible. But perhaps the validator distribution will not decrease to a level decided to be not good enough. Just like increasing blobs gradually and follow up on validators going offline, maybe theres a way of keep decreasing a variable in the issuance curve if a measurement of validator distribution gets is > sufficient for "maximum decentralization".. or something similar?

From my personal experience as someone who was a miner and fully supported the switch to PoS -I can say the psychological shift is real. When I mined coins, I tracked what I paid for them and wouldn’t sell below cost, because that would be a loss.

With PoS, I view validator rewards as passive income. I keep my original ETH balance and treat the rewards as disposable. I generally try to compound it but if I need cash, I sell them because they feel like income. I even sold some investment properties to convert the equity into validators, thinking the yield would be like rental income. But I’ve come to realize it’s not rental yield - it’s dilution of my own equity.

I know a lot of people don’t want to admit this because it validates what PoW supporters were saying but that’s my honest experience.

I still think POS is better but the issuance needs to be minimal because i feel like its just a tax on all ETH holders and the more that is paid just dilutes my equity even more. I also believe that's why we have been down only since the merge

You’re not wrong, but I’m not sure this is the best way of looking at it. (Even if I agree with a minimal viable issuance)

Higher yields to some degree create demand, the amount we can unfortunately only guess. But we can probablt all agree that:
0 net issuance with 5% yield is more attractive than
0 net issuance with 1% yield

But hard to say if:
-1% net annual supply change with 3% yield is better than
-2% net annual supply change with 1% yield

In terms of narrative I believe that -1.0% or -1.2% is not as important levels as. -0.1% vs +0.1%, so just looking at it from a binary perspective; positive or negative is the imporant thing and IMO the philosofphy should be (as me mega post above)
1. Lower issuance as much as possible
2. Get usage & burn fees to push it below 0

If still negative issuance, a discussion could be made if it’s worth changing a variable in the issuance curve to please stakers, but also as in my long post, we need to monitor staker distribution to understand where their limits for taking validators offline are.

I agree with you if I know for sure that 2 is better for demand than 1 of the examples below, which one is better for lowering the supply is the easy part.
1) -1% net annual supply change with 3% yield
2) -2% net annual supply change with 1% yield

Of my “normie” friends I know two of them prefer Solana over ETH with one of the key factors: they think they get 8% yield on Solana (they’re not even staking and I think they are getting yield anyways).

So when for example ETH Staking ETFs are introduced in US, I’m sure lots of people will be more impressed with them if they give 3% interest rate (or however tradfi will call it) than 1%, and more people don’t even know about, understand the impact of issuance.

So to some degree, high issuance and staking rewards create some type of demand.
I’m not smart enough to understand the degrees of it and how it will affect the order books.

But I think Ethereum needs to do everything possible to keep the issuance as low as possible, then communication/marketing is important to educate on the benefits and with this make up for potential reduced demand from lowering staking yields.

With the current issuance and burn, BTC will have a lower issuance after next halving and we’re alsmost on pair now.

messages.text:
Digital scarcity is pretty much not the value add of bitcoin, IMO. Immutability, ossification and decentralisation is.

They’re happy to post empty blocks because in their mind BTC the coin is the product and the network needs to ossify and consequently become unusable to make that narrative stick is a pretty bad one.

Eth does not have the luxury to ossify anytime soon. It is decentralised and if issuance is reduced, that decentralisation will die out as vertically/horizontally integrated centralised entities can provide inorganic yield to incentivise stake. Which means the value proposition is gone.

Demand fixes this.

When doing business, I ask: what’s the biggest problem I can solve? Bigger problems command bigger rewards.

Right now, the world’s biggest problem isn’t building new payment rails or decentralized apps - it’s preserving wealth. People are trying to protect themselves from inflation, high taxes, government overreach, and geopolitical chaos.

Store of Value isn’t just important- it’s urgent. Solve that and you capture the greatest demand.

Ethereum is more valuable if no entity controls it, if you ~zero issuance, imho you are just giving up and handing over control of eth fork choice to ~three parties or less. I think that’s value destructive not value accretive long term, low issuance rate or otherwise.

Tl;dr: meme attached.

Well - Provable scarcity (or even the illusion of it for the foreseeable future) is an acceptable value proposition as prime holder motivation is not necessarily to participate in the functioning of the network, but beating fiat inflation on a risk-adjusted basis & retain/grow their relative purchasing power.

Once you really understand the following - it becomes much more clear that staking emissions are essentially seignorage income, which economists argue is an inflation tax levied by govts on their citizens where revenue collection falls short.

Some credit expansion is necessary & healthy for growing economies (& inflation that comes with it is acceptable)- but the real objective is that onchain economy must keep growing in an active manner, non-productive (purely speculative) or otherwise.

These are risk/growth assets at the EOD.
That's one of one of the contributing factors why ETH has underperformed relative to BTC & even SOL in the high interest rate environment.

Look at ETHBTC, SOLETH and SOLBTC charts & you'll understand user motivations clearly (provable scarcity> relative growth).

Exporting the gas token to L2's while is directionally correct for rollup centric roadmap, however - not if it happens at the expense of reduced L1 assets issuance or active liquidity migration to L2's.

The marketing behind ETH2.0 was brilliant, it told people they needed to own ETH to run a validator, which after the merge became the only way to earn more ETH. This created strong demand. On top of that, EIP-1559 was pitched as making ETH potentially deflationary, branding it as “ultrasound money” and even a better store of value than BTC. That narrative is what attracted me to Ethereum.

While the merge was delayed, I didn’t mind becuause I was accumulating ETH through my validators, and the asset was becoming scarcer thanks to the burn. Eventually the broader crypto market started to rally and ETH’s price climbed.

But then came the Dencun upgrade. The introduction of blobs significantly reduced the burn, and ETH has become inflationary again since then. I think this shift weakened ETH’s appeal as a long-term store of value.

The average staker looks at ETH yield of 3% versus a US high yield savings account at 4% and says I'll take the 4%. In order to reduce rewards, the narrative has to be focused on net yield. I.e. The ETH narrative would be deflation of 1% while stakers earn 1.5% and the real yield is 2.5%.

If everyone suddenly had double the ETH, I think price would drop probably more than half. It’s not just about numbers, it’s the psychology. Sudden inflation kills the scarcity narrative and people start offloading, especially those who were in it for the SOV.

Conversely if everyone had half, I think price would go more than double. Scarcity goes up, people feel poorer, and no one wants to sell. That drives up demand and price, especially if future issuance is expected to stay low.

text:
Exactly. The pertinent questions that need to be asked & answered is :

1) Is the L1 mainnet implementation, the best representation of hub-spoke model of rollup centric roadmap we're hoping for (& not poorly co-opting Cosmos).

2) Is it the best smart contract platform to enable and empower the next generation of slightly more complex applications.

3) How is L1 security premium been valued here if liquidity & asset issuance gets exported to slightly less secure L2's (that are experimental multisigs today than Stage 2 rollups upgrading with hard-forks).

4) Are we really tinkering with monetary policy w/without looking at the applications, activity that has been dominating the space.

5) How is virtual asset value socially perceived and accepted? 

I think most people here know the answer to these questions already & even the validity of rollup centric roadmap (i.e. it is directionally correct - but just too early).

My endgame vision of ETH is :

Retain liquidity on L1, upgrade it enough that it's a decent orchestration middleware for other
, a good lifetime fee mechanism that can perpetually bankroll your Treasury if quadrillions of volume is moved onchain (& you charge few bps in fees).

At this point - I don't think it's controversial to say that many of general purpose/specialised L2's might go to ZERO bc they have zero incubator premium (much less applications themselves have premium).

SoV premium competition with many of these high perf chains has defaulted to the lowest common denominator userbase & quality of liquidity - (memecoins, gambling) which is also a good thing tbh.

Strong incubation culture will be of importance.

Infinite supply overhang, little blockspace demand - very little valuable apps.

Defi does have long-term staying power & there's long-term innovation there, interoperability will be the greatest strength AND weakness to the L1 premium (it will command long-term premium of its own).

I have some loose ideas on what I'd probably do differently if it were upto me. 😅

messages.text:
And you're rarely likely to get L2's to act strongly in the interest of Ethereum (even if we introduce based rollups or preconfs) unless 
1) They have Ethereum like token distribution.
2) Or have a clear PMF to not need a token for governance or cryptoeconomic in-protocol mechanism reasons (ala, ERC-20 restaking).

That is going to be a rare possibility bc the incentives are not aligned in any shape or form. 

L2's issue tokens to return liquid capital to their investors & do GTM bootstrapping (though the widespread success of this rn is widely questionable). 

So if the sequencer isn't capturing substantial fees at economies of scale & MEV goes to L1 - fee switch isn't going to benefit equity holders in any reasonable way & a down only L2 token is the only secondary recourse (with its own set of consequences).

The sole purpose of rollup centric roadmap was L1 to act as liquidity hub & slower orchestration middleware for "highly specialised" L2 blockspace that may or may not inherit the L1's security guarantees for the set of tradeoffs they make.

What we have rn is worse than Cosmos IBC 2.0 & the L1 + L2 are both losing collectively. 

User 093 farming, forked User 049pps are rampant - and incubation culture is really suffering.

I'm not 100% sure if we will get synchronous composability w most L2's either (some, sure). 

Rollup centric roadmap is directionally correct though IMO (meant to grow with economies of scale) - I'm just not sure if there's consensus rn around what will be a simple & elegant design standard for long-term fees for the L1.

Solana will have LSR, an Enshrined AMM chain or liquidity routing hub will probably use onchain liquidity for economic security or charge few bps in fees. 

So this is sort of an open-ended question : How is reworking blob fees, peerUser 049S improve the structural demand of things wen onchain activity hasn't meaningfully grown? 

Are any potential solutions simple, elegant & long-term sustainable? (Harberger taxes to L2's, default swap fees, passing the cost to consumer).

Happy to hear your thoughts guys on what kind of an endgame are we chasing here.

messages.text:
I’m not denying that there’s strong growth and use cases for stablecoins, especially in emerging markets where access to USD or stable banking is limited. That makes a lot of sense.

But I’m looking at this from a Western consumer's point of view where credit cards offer convenience, strong consumer protections, insurance, and widespread merchant acceptance. Most people here aren’t going to give that up for lower fees unless there's a massive incentive or the current system breaks down.

The argument that it's like paying cash onchain is interesting, but we also need to ask: why is paying with cash becoming less common in developed countries? Because convenience and protections often matter more than privacy or avoiding fees for the average person.

I’m not saying the growth will stop, but we should be clear-eyed about where the demand is coming from and whether that demand justifies scaling to billions of users globally. If the use case is mostly EM or crypto native activity, that’s still big but it’s not the same as replacing Visa or Mastercard in NYC, Sydney or London

Might make sense eventually - but there are lot of deep rooted social problems like internet penetration, mobile phones that'll need fixing before we get there. 

My background is from TradFi & none of these projections make rational sense to me. 🙃

And why would Western Union L2 or Visa/Mastercard be launching onchain  abandon their core business unit function for minimal benefit of borderless tx's? Blockchains are IaaS at EOD, but of complementary nature.

It's a diversification strategy for their operations, not really a strong, growing profit center. Settlement delays for high value transactions are not a bug, but feature - there's compliance factor involved.

Even if they do - wouldn't they prefer that customers etc paid fees in their own native token (gasless paymasters, like Coinbase wallet does with USDC - or charge a swap fee) or their own ledger.

PS : My arguments are made with the assumption that blockchains are a simply a small, emerging & growing subset of financial digitization wave - not the centerpiece of it.

I've invested in fintech startups outside of crypto for quite a few years, i.e. payment processing firms, small startups doing micro finance & basically operating neobanks with digital wallets (w/o the crypto element).

Onchain primitives are great for self-custody & optionality - to protect against the downside of fractional banking & insolvency - not a substitute w/o FDIC insurance though.

Not sure reg will allow stablecoin issuers to pass yield to holders, you might need a decentralised primitive after all (& wouldn't be able to promote it as stablecoin though).

The onchain neobanks that we do have are like AAVE which pass on the yield.

To choose stables over banks - crypto has to be fundamentally safer, robust and simply better - structural demand creation on consumer side to make the switch. 

I see wishful thinking, which is good - but is it pragmatic enough, idk. Choosing a permissionless ledger like Ethereum or even Sol might also tell to skip on infrastructure costs, I'd give you that.

There's a reason I am very bullish on dominant interoperability protocols in the long run btw (as a trader) even with high competition - Clear PMF (supports high velocity capital movement that can achieve economies of scale even at marginal bps of fees).

It's all tokens, liquidity & swaps at EOD - rollups are mostly bridges. 🫡

What is clear to me that while scaling L1 activity will be of priority - it will eventually hit roadblock, which is where L2's will have to step in.

The only issue is our in-protocol fee mechanisms kinda suck rn (blobs) & nothing concrete in play for interop. Zero premium for ETH User 049 or security guarantees really - as we've pushed for L2 adoption a bit prematurely.

Something must definitely be done about this (in-protocol mechanism, acquiring strategic stake to make sure Ethereum stays competitive enough like our great higher educational institutions).

Do it & Ethereum wins sustainably. Most of the pain points about losing value accrual go away. 😀

Otherwise - you're paying 2-3% as seignorage income to least productive capital for economic security, which is just flat inflation tax w/o relative GDP growth or fees (tax revenue) to show for.

Getting beat by centralised high performance chains competing on lowest common denominator liquidity (who have kinda figured out the monetary policy).

Choose balanced budget, not Sri Lankan economics - getting into the weeds of incubating apps better, and maybe mimetic SoV premium will return & bleed against BTC stops (~which has to worry about security budget issues into far future).

EF has 3-4 yrs of runway (atleast better than 2020 conditions though), but it solely becomes a battle of attrition then if stressed market conditions persist for longer. 

I know nothing, and I'm pretty sure lot of people here much intelligent than me will figure it out.🤝❤️

Thou who shall fix the narrative & structure around Ethereum's multi-dimensional fee future - shall inherit the world.

I am not positively convinced as well whatever we have planned to fix blobs in  upcoming updates will have a large marginal effect in saving "ETH is money" narrative.

Right now - Ethereum gets none of the upside in interop/security premium w centralised multisigs (centralised relayers & solvers capture most of it), little to no fee premium when people deposit liquidity, net L1 asset issuance is on the down low & gasless paymasters exist (weakened ETH gas token premium) - real-time proving is still a little far off.

One of the few times I'd say that too much optionality is a bad thing & it hurts Ethereum vs vertical scaling.

The story also needs simplicity & reliable predictability for L1's source of fees (& these fees is +ve proof of "useful" work tied to productive economic activity other than aspects of running the network - consensus, execution, proving rewards)

This is the reason why Sol has ETH beat recently amongst many things w memecoin launchpad craze (just like NFT era fees, locked up Sol creates a burn effect, MEV redistribution to stakers, toxic or otherwise is a onchain productivity tax redistributed to stakers by a third party...which incentivised users to participate...a good airdrop was just additional wealth creation).

I think we'd have an easier time convincing interop protocols to opt-in & share portion of their income for high value tx's if we acquire some controlling stake programmatically each time those tx's happen.

L0 airdrop claim was quite a successful public goods funding exp for Protocol Guild in a way, but maybe it can be turned into something scalable?

messages.text:
I completely agree with you. Ethereum's optionality and modularity have created an environment where value leaks outward instead of flowing back to the base layer. Right now, it feels like the more we scale, the less we reinforce ETH as money.

I'd actually go even a step further:
I’m starting to think that giving users endless L2 choices might have been a mistake. Instead of supporting dozens of fragmented ecosystems with their own tokens, bridges, and fee structures, Ethereum should seriously consider enshrining a single decentralized Layer 2 that is directly tied to ETH security and value accrual.

A decentralized, enshrined ETH L2 could:
- Drastically simplify the user experience
- Recapture fees and activity directly to ETH
- Strengthen the ETH as money narrative by tying real economic activity tightly back to the asset
- Preserve decentralization while providing a clear default for users.

We already have the proof points: Solana’s vertical integration works. Users respond to clarity, low friction, and direct value flows. Right now, Ethereum's sprawl risks losing both mindshare and monetary premium to vertically integrated competitors and if we lose our first mover advantage to Solana then its game over.

It might upset some of the current ecosystem players, but in the long run, aligning the roadmap around a shared settlement and value-capture layer feels like a survival move and I think thats whats needed to turn ethereum around

messages.text:
I'm not in the reduce issuance club either - improving the staking rate & bumping institutional participation there will in a way compress the staking yield further.

This is what Etherealize, Danny & Vivek need to convince institutions of.

But to call PoS network staking yield for providing economic security as sustainable issuance is a misnomer too, bc it's always going to dilutive cost weighed as rel growth of the network.

The actual competition is from these other networks who have sought ETH's moment of relative weakness as opportunity - to shill the moneyness narrative for their networks by cutting emissions more quickly than originally intended (Sol, TIA).

I don't think a bigger conversation is warranted now for cutting issuance - but there needs to be one around how L1 achieves a persistent, scalable fee premium for L1 execution, interop and it's liquidity so that the term "L2's are extending Ethereum/leveraging ETH's security mean something in fixed & dynamic fee terms.

The story around this needs to be clear as day.

 The story everyone got was "This is Sri Lankan economics" at play for the L1 giving away its moat rather than..."we're introducing efficiencies over time to scale L1 & L2 activity to pass benefits to consumer"

just like Google did with its free cloud storage per email account (which started at 1GB back in the day & is now at 15).

This sort of subsidization was rationally powered by a net increase in onchain usage from users YoY & perfecting sustainable unit economics - not achieved by breaking it.

Still only 50/50 bullish that Fusaka EIP'S will fix blob pricing - do suspect some L2's will continue to underpay going forward.
