messages.text:
With stablecoin regulation passing in multiple countries, banks now finally have the legal clarity to issue stablecoins to their customers. But for global interoperability, they can’t build their own chains or rely on a chain controlled by another bank. They’ll need a neutral, decentralized chain. Ethereum is the obvious choice, but L1 is too slow and expensive for mass payments, so they’ll need a scalable L2.

Rather than having every bank spin up its own fragmented rollup, wouldn’t it make more sense for Ethereum to build an enshrined shared rollup, optimized for fast and cheap payments, but still general-purpose and open to all use cases? This would give banks and enterprises a neutral platform to build on, protect Ethereum’s network effects, and avoid losing stablecoin volumes to competing ecosystems.

Curious if anyone’s thinking about this or if it’s too late given how much has already been built privately. Should we be prioritizing an enshrined rollup now before fragmentation becomes too entrenched?

Back from some time off, and I feel like i should recap some important points that don't look to be highlighted in the last chunk of activity in this chat:

- "Once stake approaches 100% the rewards for home stakers or anyone else approaches zero." This only applies to the ~5% of the network that solo stakes. For the other ~95% that receive delegation, their commission is real at any issuance rate. If we pretend 90+% of validators don't exist, or don't model their returns

correctly, we're not going to get the economics right for a change. 

- One/a small group of parties controlling ethereum's fork choice is a soft-compromise of the chain, and something we should design to prevent. I do not believe we will have the coordination ability to socially-slash these parties, particularly because of the amount of retail stake that would be destroyed for a decision taken by their agents (likely under government duress). We should not let ourselves end up in that position. (personally i view this as a far, far bigger risk than raw eth being subverted by a wrapper, and I view capping proposals as exacerbating this risk much more than what they achieve in preventing single-LST dominance). 

- Doing nothing about ePBS/mev-burn means that the biggest pools of capital make the most reward. This pushes the chain into a bad gini coefficient. It also encourages single-LST dominance. Fixing this would mitigate the bleed of long tail staking products.

- Doing nothing about the interminable exit queue pushes allocators into liquid wrappers like LSTs. A protocolised price to exit stake would reduce the dependence on deeply liquid centralised platforms (CB and binance) and LSTs for staking. The fact that long term holders (like staked etfs) can't native stake is a big problem for Ethereum's decentralisation, and one we could and should do (have done) something about. 

- The marginal cost of running extra stake is near zero. As a result, commission rates are near zero (<=1%). Small operators are failing to stay afloat in this world and the gini and nakamoto coefficients are suffering. You need a billion dollars in delegation to run a node operator that pays a human a real salary to run the nodes. Artificially raising the commission rates in a free market (non-dPoS chain) is not very feasible, so there is little we can do from a protocol design perspective here (that I can think of), but the social layer could play a role. 

- Running a validator costs hundreds of dollars per year minimum. High fixed costs means the long tail of operators will leave the network first in a capped environment or one with downward pressure on real rates. This harms the gini coefficient. It is more profitable for a solo staker to delegate to an LST than it is to run their own node already. 

- Gini coefficients and nakamoto coefficients are better measures of ethereum's decentralisation than staking ratio. "Economic security" without decentralisation is worth nothing. (see sui). As a thought experiment, which is worse; The chain's fork choice is controlled by coinbase, but only 20% of eth is staked. Or the chain needs 20+ operators to collude to control fork choice, but 60% percent of eth is staked? I believe the former is less secure than the latter, though not everyone in this chat agrees it seems, hence the mis-alignment and why we go in circles.

So many points to get into here but I particularly want to push back against this strawman: 

"As a thought experiment, which is worse; The chain's fork choice is controlled by coinbase, but only 20% of eth is staked. Or the chain needs 20+ operators to collude to control fork choice, but 60% percent of eth is staked?"
 
Coinbase or any other centralised entity is much more likely to dominate in the case where there is excess yield. If yields are matched to the risk/cost of capital (i.e. very low given the rarity of slashing and the liquidity offered by LSTs) and stakers do not gain an edge in block building (because of attester/proposer separation), then the people who stake will be those who actually want to protect the protocol rather than extract from it.

There is no reason to believe that high issuance will keep the validator set decentralised, it's just a bigger incentive for the big players to capture as much as they can.

messages.text:
> Coinbase or any other centralised entity is much more likely to dominate in the case where there is excess yield

Walk me through how you see this working. and probably how you define 'excess'. I don't consider an arbitrary staking ratio % as sufficient security, and above that, excess (see strawman). I could be open to considering above a certain nakamoto co-efficient excess. 3 digits+? 4 digits+? but can this be done without being dPoS? 

> stakers do not gain an edge in block building (because of attester/proposer separation)

We agree here. Spiky mev means the biggest validators gain an edge here and that needs adressing. We'll never mitigate the centralisation forces with only cost control if revenue (and liquidity) are unequal. 

> the people who stake will be those who actually want to protect the protocol rather than extract from it

Do you mean the people that will run the nodes, or the people that will delegate? I infer you mean delegation. Where i have a problem is node operation. The marginal delegate to the biggest pool/entity is no good to the protocol (we probably agree there i'd guess). The marginal node operator (on the cumulative 50% of stake line) is important, and what i consider to be protecting the protocol. You do not retain a meaningful amount of independent nodes when break even is as low as the largest of entities can sustain/subsidise.  

> There is no reason to believe that high issuance will keep the validator set decentralised, it's just a bigger incentive for the big players to capture as much as they can

Do you think the inverse holds up? 'There is no reason to believe that low issuance will centralise the validator set' ? If not, why not? 

I'm not saying increasing issuance will increase decentralisation, but I am saying decreasing issuance will decrease decentralisation, particularly the long tail. What I am trying to get across is that to increase decentralisation we need to flatten the expected return between delegating to a tiny indie staker/lst vs the largest, and having the liquidity profile of the long tail be as close as feasible to the largest pools of capital. (Commission rates and costs of operation are also important but less so)

text: Took some time to review this now, posted it here:

A few points about the modeling assumptions:

1. The "real yield zero-crossings" can be interesting as markers of when stakers stop gaining share of supply if costs are paid in ETH, but they are not an indifference point between staking and holding.
2. Further, the x-axis "gap" between real yield zero-crossings for different staking types does not tell us anything about the resulting composition of the staking set under a specific reward curve.
3. An important reason is that the equilibrium, at which all stakers receive the same nominal yield, must be modeled jointly.
4. Under the suggested perfectly elastic supply curves, the joint equilibrium will only feature the staking type with the lowest cost, regardless of the reward curve.
5. An ideal model will treat stakers as heterogeneous, with a resulting distribution of reservation yields within each type. Such a model will produce upward-sloping supply curves, from which a realistic equilibrium composition of the staking set can be derived.

messages.text:
In response to User 015's great article, I spent some time taking the temperature of how folks are feeling about issuance reduction.

In short, it's not good. There is widespread opposition to changing monetary policy in any way.

Instead of trying to discuss why that's the case, let me give a simple recommendation: 

The political struggle is lost in this era.

For people who believe in the necessity of reducing staking participation (as I do), the task now may be to lay firm technical groundwork so that we are ready when the political opportunity presents itself.

In particular, eip1559 benefited from having been fully specified years ahead of activation. That gave it time to bake politically and drive neutrality and expectation of implementation via ongoing research of the concrete proposal and not just hypothetical scenarios. We should do the same here- arrive at the concrete proposal asap and begin the long road to activation.

text:
Hi all, sorry to drop a long one, but wanted to weigh in on some points in the above. tl;dr i support legitimacy building for a different ethereum that needs different actors to be compensated. I think the most important KPI for ‘is this issuance working’ is whether the chain’s nakamoto co-efficient is going in the right or wrong direction. A high staking ratio with good diversity is far more secure than a targeted ratio that has whittled down the validator set to the largest, lowest cost operators. That risks intentional compromise and unintentional black swan issues (forks/hacks/etc). 

> The core issue is whether ethereum and ETH are ready to last a thousand years and run the whole global economy. 
> The answer is "no" because the current issuance curve was effectively a mistake.

I agree with the first part of this (and it is what we should optimise for even beyond my advocation for nakamoto as a measure of success). However you’re not the first to call the original curve a ‘mistake’, and I’d like to add my understanding of why it was deliberate, not a bug, or mistake, or that they didn’t know what they were doing. 

We don’t know what the ‘right’ ratio is exactly. We don’t know how much it costs to maintain that ratio. We don’t know how to keep that ratio decentralised. So given all that, they chose a curve that starts at like >20%, quickly drops to sub 3% real, and curves out smoothly to 0% real at 100% staked. Not picking a demarcation line allowed the market to find its own equilibrium. Choosing to print extra eth the higher the ratio goes was deliberate to prevent the big CEXs pricing out small operation.

> to ensure the protocol states a preference about how much stake it actually wants.

Quality > quantity. how decentralised the validator set is more important than its size (within the extremes).

> One thing we've learned is that there are very good reasons to expect vanilla ETH in the app layer to become extremely rare if we allow staking to continue on its current course.

Considering the rsEth + defi blow up we’ve experienced this week. Do you really think we’re going to see almost all stake in LSTs to avoid a ~1.5% worst case scenario dilution? (lower than gold, cash, bitcoin for now, etc).  

> There's also an important relationship with shipping fast finality in terms of the potential, need to reduce the validator set size.

Reducing it by killing off the long tail of decentralised setups is not a good long term decision imo. 

> The definite crisis is that ethereum is structurally much weaker and riskier when 66% to 95% of ETH is staked.

Its relative imo. What about if ethereum is run by 2 or 3 parties due to capping hollowing out the market, and they start to censor their fork choice votes? e.g. what happened on gnosis with balancer. Ethereum is basically a censorable corporate chain from that point on. 

> What I do support is planning excellently for the future contingency of staking inflows not slowing down and steadily reaching toxic levels

I agree here, ways we can plan include; 1. Favour decentralisation,

might marginally favour choosing decentralised setups. 
. Favour native staking, if people aren’t all in upgradeable liquid wrappers that might help. A price to exit stake is needed there. Track the market rate for delegating stake as best possible. Track the market rate for operating a certain amount of eth. 
Track the gini co-efficient of withdrawal addresses of stake to ensure they don’t become too vulnerable to a single point of failure (which is imo what most people actually worry about when it comes to high staking ratios). Come up with a plan for how block building and proving can be credibly permissionless and decentralised, and work towards funding that with issuance to protect it etc. 

> Solo stakers will always be a minority, but the fact that they exist is one of the things that gives Ethereum a better claim to permissionlessness and neutrality than any rival blockchain

This statement feels good, but ultimately push comes to shove, how decentralised the group that chooses fork choice (>51% of stake weight), is what dictates if a network is sufficiently decentralised. otherwise you’re just PoA + verifier nodes for all the good it does you. 

> how does this discussion take account of the prover stuff?

That’s ultimately the uncomfortable compromise i think all this group could make; proving won’t be free, free market block building will also be centralising, we’ve a transformative post quantum upgrade ahead of us (that proving could ship with in theory (it’ll stagger)). That’s where I think the community should spend its social capital on achieving buy in on a change to issuance and what we socially think sufficient distribution of control over of the validator set looks like.

I am looking forward to reading your take on this.
We shouldn't be afraid of changing the monetary policy went it is not benefiting the security of the network. Historically we changed the monetary policy as in "the issuance " 6 times already. I think the framing with the FED is not correct, the central bank has a mandate "control the inflation (make sure it's not above this

)" sometimes it has a secondary, lower priority additional mandate "support the economic growth if the inflation is contained" . The target of the central bank in term of inflation is what guides it's monetary policy: more or less mandatory deposits for banks, tweaks in this or that interest rate , buy or sell of assets etc. The monetary policy is constantly changing and adjusting to match the deviation of the target.

Ethereum has a reward curve. I believe what you are referring to at EthCC is a moment where I said something like "we should adopt a max issuance target, in protocol. That would be our definitive, final, long term, everlasting commitment to not grow the supply of ETH above this target per year. For example, max 0.5%. It's easy to communicate, it's showing maturity versus other chains, and more importantly we have enough to secure Ethereum with this max issuance. Now, how we would get to this target in terms of which reward curve get us there is a wide design space. There are several classes of curves that can accommodate a max issuance target

text.text: . We can endlessly debate on which curve against another but the good news is, if we realize that we picked the wrong curve because it ended being too aggressive for some categories of stakers, we can always change the curve later while still commiting to the max issuance target

text:
"

My point was that an extreme position like "we can only change it once so we shouldn't do anything if we are not 100% sure nothing will go bad" can not stand or prevent us from correcting the negative externalities of the current curve

It was believed among the researchers (correct me if I'm wrong EFer from the protocol teams) that liquid staking would not gain meaningful traction, it was also believed that the rewards might not be high enough to attract enough ETH at stake. es Lido like all the staking services making money by taking a cut on the yield generated will be  impacted by a reduction of the yield. It's not good for Ethereum to be in a regime of 30%+ ETH at stake, let alone a regime of 35%+ long entry queue with no clear sign on stopping at all.
Staking is Operational risks + Liquidity risks+ Opportunity cost risks ; the market weights all these risks and expects a yield to compensate for them. The equilibrium will be reached when the market finds the reservation yield of the marginal staker. We are clearly far from this reservation yield and our current reward curve has a minimum yield of 1.6% (when the whole circulating supply is at stake).

Ethereum should not change the issuance curve until new architectural changes are set in motion.

Ideally, a good SoV will be something that has low tail inflation & net emissions fluctuate within a % band range (where it's deflationary & inflationary) as needed w time. -1%/+1, -2%, +2% - credit expansion & contraction via interest rate control, as needed.

You do not want to Ethereum to be observed by the outside world as technocratic feudal state where everyone is doing everything in their power to fuck around with interest rates, but ignore the one thing that matters (increase velocity of onchain assets issued at the base layer, and generate economic surplus commerce...ie.. goods and services being priced in

, any elastic and inelastic changes happening onchain).

If 5yrs of price action/suppression by sophisticated capital positioning, insufficient growth in achieving economies of scale despite EIP-1559 reduction of net new emissions & tail inflation going up only since 22' hasn't taught anyone anything, let this be a good reminder.

messages.text:
I have moderate to high conviction that we shouldn't mess with staking emissions. Every time you "fiddle" with ETH's monetary policy, you reset the shot clock on it being considered a credibly neutral, relatively ossified store of value. That being said, here are some high-level rebuttals to the most common arguments:

1. ETH is overpaying for security.
This is a dumb argument. You can't be too secure, and recent events have borne this out. Further, the more ETH that's staked, the more friction there is to sell it. In addition, for ETH there's a pretty high coefficient of holding from staking (vs mining) - unlike BTC miners who are forced to sell to cover operating expenses, many ETH stakers are content to let their ETH compound over time.

2. A single LST could monopolize the ecosystem.
This is a highly speculative take, and could occur even in the presence of capped stake. 

3. Too much staking = token dilution. Token dilution is bad b/c it increases selling pressure on ETH.
If you decompose the drivers of ETH's price, the EF's ability to get its shit together to deliver network upgrades, the ETH community's ability to build apps that create real world demand, and the broader investor community's perception of ETH as a store of value are collectively like 10-100x+ more important than the marginal selling pressure caused by increased staking. (And as I mentioned, this selling pressure likely isn't even very large given the holding coefficient.)

4. Loss of monetary premium if too much ETH is staked.
This argument is incoherent and dumb. Monetary premium comes from the broader investor community's perception of ETH, and staked ETH and raw ETH are essentially the same asset.

5. Solo stakers are forced out because of income tax issues.
Another dubious argument. Any income tax that would have to be paid by solo stakers also likely needs to be paid by LST stakers. Taxes also vary widely by jurisdiction. 

The arguments for issuance reduction strike me as theoretical and path-dependent (when in fact, numerous different paths to multiple staking equilibria exist, many of which present zero problems). When there's actual evidence that a high staking ratio is a threat to ETH, I'll be more open to this. Until then, we have far bigger issues to worry about.

text: Hi

, great article - especially the visuals.

Since you asked for feedback, let me approach it from a simple lens: “what is the problem”, what are the constraints, and for a suggested solution, ask “does it solve the problem?”.

I see multiple concerns: Too much staking - it is going to 100%, high staking ratio leads to security degradation, solo stakers get pushed out, LST / financialization risk. 

Then, a single lever - issuance reduction-  is treated as a solution to all those problems and I am not convinced this holds. 

Let me break down the problems and thoughts on each of them:

I agree that extremely high participation is undesirable and that the issuance curve should not incentivize it. Although I doubt staking will approach 100% in practice (given ETH needed for CEX liquidity, DeFi usage, L2s, paying fees, and many users just hodl, I doubt it would ever go above 70-75%), it still makes sense to not allow this to happen.

This requires a solid and well-thought out way to determine the target range (not throwing random numbers such as 25%, 33%, 50%), evaluating constraints / tradeoffs such as “impact on validator decentralization”. I don’t see this happening here.

Here I struggle to see how issuance reduction improves their position. Lower rewards would bring the break-even point closer, not further away, so the problem likely worsens. More broadly, solo staker viability is driven by structural factors (costs, complexity, protocol design) other than issuance. And most of the expected -not fully specified- changes in staking such as valset size cap, APS, etc. may challenge solo staking further (higher min requirement, no EL rewards), making it even less clear how an issuance change at this stage benefits solo stakers without taking into account other moving pieces.

I don’t see a mechanism by which issuance materially shifts the balance between LSTs and solo stakers (LST dominance might exist at 10%, 20% staking ratios as well). If anything, reducing viability of onchain solutions risks pushing users towards custodial alternatives.  If LSTs become less attractive, the dominant substitution is unlikely to be solo staking, but CEX staking — which could worsen centralization. Also, as you note, much of the recent growth is driven by ETFs and institutional flows, which are largely independent of LST dynamics.

To me, the only problem which can be solved via issuance update (among the ones you mention in the post) is the excessive staking participation.  A revised issuance curve could be designed explicitly around that goal, with careful consideration of its impact on validator composition and decentralization.

My issue with this line of argumentation is that I don’t find the idea that 20-30% capped stake rate doesn’t result in an even more brittle Ethereum convincing. It seems like there’s an imagined outcome at 20-30% eth staked which is better than an imaged outcome at 70%+ staked, and you’re taking the worst possible outcome at the higher stake rate and comparing it to the best possible outcome at 30% staked and then saying Ethereum is better for it. The reality is that these outcomes are very path dependent and the pressures that exist for centralization exist at both ends but IMO are more pronounced in a “capped” system at a low stake rate because it essentially ends up working like cutting the market from the neck down. 

1) I think POS actually resembles representative democracy quite a bit, and in general democracies are healthier when those making decisions (validators in the network) are empowered with as much of the underlying representation of the network as possible (i.e. higher voter turnout generally leads to healthier democracies). The more ETH that is staked, the higher the overlap of users & holders & stakers is, i.e. it’s essentially a way to reduce the principal agent problem between staking solutions and the their users (stakers) (because stakers have more choice), as well as between validators/stakers and the rest of the network’s users. An Ethereum where only 20-30% of the network participates in securing it it, which may well eventually operated by a handful of corporate entities most of which will be in the US, is not really representative of Ethereum as a whole. 

2) Moreover, introducing a cap is in practical terms a one-way door type decision; if it turns out that a low stake rate was a bad idea, you cannot revive the market just be removing the cap. Capping the stake rate means that solutions with higher marginal cost (e.g. decentralized ones vs centralized onces) essentially cannot compete in the long-run, because artificially constraining supply means that only the cheapest (or with the ability to make money elsewhere) suppliers will prevail — i.e. the market is not large enough for demand which has wider price elasticity to effect its preference. Once these decentralized players (who have higher costs, longer time to execution, and are disadvantaged from a regulatory perspective) exit the market, I think it’s nigh impossible to bring them (or new ones) back.

3) > There are also no ETH left unstaked to come and defend neutrality by lowering the marketshare of large stakers. Slashing events for a large actor behaving badly or censoring some transaction are not credible. Ethereum has failed at being a credibly neutral chain. 

I agree this is the case at 100%, I don’t think it’s that much of a problem at 50-60% staked (i.e. 25-33% is enough to fend off an attack which would be 2-3x as expensive as in the 20-30% stake rate scenario). Most importantly, though, in most cases where you’d need ETH to come back in to defend against some kind of attack then it’s highly unlikely that it’s possible for this ETH to enter fast enough to do much. The damage will have been done, and at a fraction of the cost that it would have otherwise taken had the cap not been in effect. The only real solution to validator set capture at a low stake rate where 3-4 entities get forced by some jurisdiction to implement censorship is a UASF, and then you’ve basically destroyed the network once that happens as credible neutrality goes out the window. Conversely, high stake rate means that a larger subset of users/holders is able actively able to participate (“vote with their feet/ETH”) in enforcing its ideals through the selection of the staking solution/provider that matches them. The more this number approach 100%, the more one can state that the underlying validator set is representative of the Ethereum populace and its preferences, and the less likely an attack through the staking mechanism is to occur.

4) I think the idea of MVI in terms of “optimal security” from a technical and economic perspective is a bit of a red herring. I agree there’s diminishing returns for every new dollar paid in terms of how much security you get, although I don’t think you really get negative returns at any point, but efficiency is not a good metric when trying to figure out what’s “best" because once you have a catastrophic security event it’s all over. What you want to do is reduce the likelihood of something bad happening as much as possible, and I don’t think that’s the case when approaching the problem in this way. I made this analogy when we had the debate in Cannes, but if you think of security as a form of defense spending, then “optimally” you would spend 1 dollar more than your adversary, but in reality that’s not how that works at all. To deter an attacker you have to make it as impossibly costly as possible for them to attack you, and this usually is only possible via “overspending” on defense.

Don’t want to get into the dilution and moneyness arguments now. I agree telegram is not the best medium for these types of convos and this message is already huge. I think there’s very likely a natural equilibrium somewhere between 50-70% of stake (and another one around 40-45) as the usefulness of non-staked assets increases as a result, and I don’t see higher stake rates as feasible or likely.

text: Thanks for this thoughtful feedback, I really appreciate the willingness to engage constructively on this. I'll try and respond to your sections in the order you raised them.
My contention is that

text.text: high staking ratios are the problem

text:
, and are the one thing we need to fix. All the other issues I mentioned are significantly exacerbated although not entirely caused by high staking ratios (with the exception of solo stakers being forced out, which I will come to). So if my article gave the impression that all ills are caused only by this, and that modifying issuance is a complete solution to them all, then maybe I can think about rephrasing some of that in future writing.

Also, to be clear I didn't say "issuance reduction" because it may be perfectly possible to keep issuance where it is
, but the curve

need to reduce the issuance at higher ratios than we have today.

1.

: this is a fair challenge but I would respond that the reasons you state for not approaching 100% staked will not hold if there is a dominant LST. In a very high staking ratio environment such an LST could effectively supplant ETH as the canonical token for use on CEXes, DeFi, L2s etc. To my mind replacing raw ETH in this way with an intermediated version is highly undesirable and completely unnecessary.

As for what level we should target... you're right that this has been a weakness in all the discussion/proposals so far. Researchers who have looked at this tend to conclude that there is no significant benefit to new stake once we're past perhaps the 12.5%-25% range. All seem to agree that 50% is definitely too much. But it is tricky to come up with a formula for the ideal range. In my next article I want to present a framework for reasoning this through and make a concrete recommendation for an EIP, but there will be path dependency baked in - we are where we are.

2.

the equilibrium yield will be - in dilution adjusted terms - set by the market participants with the lowest costs. I contend that these will be LST holders because they have effectively no cost of capital (the LST means their stake is effectively not locked, with capital costs at zero if the LST is treated as equivalent to ETH). The dilution-adjusted equilibrium yield will therefore be very low, and this is not something we can control. So what is the difference for solo stakers? In a 100% staked example, dilution-adjusted yield is zero (no one is really earning anything), but

text.text: solo stakers in most jurisdictions find their nominal yield is treated as income for tax purposes

text: . For example in the US, UK, Canada, France, and Australia (I am not a tax advisor but I am a solo staker in the UK) it seems that solo staker nominal yield is treated as income, and taxed annually, whereas capital gains on LSTs are only taxed on disposal, and typically at lower rates (and capital gains may be zero or negative depending on fiat prices, whereas income tax applies regardless). This creates a dramatic disparity between LST holders and solo stakers as we head to higher staking ratios under the current curve. At 100% staked, a solo staker would pay income tax on the 1.5% "yield" they are paid through issuance, when in reality all this yield was doing was compensating for dilution. So solo stakers end up effectively paying a percentage of their stake each year for the privilege of remaining in the validator set - a non-starter. On the other hand, if issuance reduces down at higher staking ratios (let's say it reaches zero at 50% staked) then we reach equilibrium somewhere in the middle of the range. Solo stakers are no longer disadvantaged relative to LST holders. I continue to believe that one of the things that differentiates Ethereum from competitors is that anybody can become a direct participant in consensus (albeit 32 ETH these days is a barrier to most individuals and needs to be lowered).

text:
Hi Jerome, glad to engage here. I'll address your points one by one:

1. Let's make the huge assumption ETH is 99% staked (1% remains to pay for transaction fees). Why do we assume it would all be held by LSTs, rather than staked in, say, exchanges? And why would slashing not be credible for one of the big LSTs? I think slashing becomes even more credible in that scenario as a warning shot to dissuade people from using correlated infrastructure. That being said, I do agree that a 100% staked ETH regime would be sub-optimal. Where I disagree is I don't believe that we're inevitably heading towards that regime. For many people, the perfect liquidity, zero counterparty risk, zero slashing risk, etc of holding raw ETH relative to holding an LST is a desirable tradeoff. 

I also don't think the dilution effect on ETH holders is that crazy. It's 1.51% at most per year before any sort of transaction fee burn. This is pretty minimal imo - gold has historically increased its supply at a rate of ~1% per year. ETH's price, driven by fundamental upgrades, usage, macro factors, etc, will cause price swings 10-100x more than 1% per year and are far more important drivers of Ethereum's success. Furthermore, as I mentioned in my first message, many of these stakers have a high marginal propensity to hold. (Especially relative to BTC miners, who have to dump almost all their BTC as soon as it's mined to pay hardware/electricity fees.) 

Fundamentally, I just don't think there will inevitably be some Gresham's Law dynamic of "bad money" (staked ETH) pushing out "good money" (raw ETH) for a massive percentage of the network at the low dilution rates we're talking about.

2. I don't think any one LST will win the "moneyness" game relative to ETH. As we speak, stETH is trading 0.5% cheaper than raw ETH is. rsETH is a fiasco. Eeth also trades at a 0.4% discount to raw ETH. These LSTs have substantial peg risks and operator risks, and very large ETH holders are well aware of them. I would agree though that in an extremely high staked ETH regime (75%+), there's a risk that LSTs would crowd out ETH in DeFi, and this would be a bad thing.  

I personally think protocol enshrined LSTs are a great solution to the potential issue of an LST crowding out ETH within DeFi and as a trading pair denominator. There's a huge interesting design space here, e.g., with rainbow staking:

. 

To reiterate, I think the "crowding out" argument generally understates the demand for raw ETH from people who are willing to eat a tiny amount of dilution in exchange for perfect liquidity and no staking counterparty/slashing risk.

My opinion, fwiw

I agree issuance is already too high (i.e. we’re already overpaying for security)

If left unchanged, I think the equilibrium staking ratio will land somewhere between 50% and 75% (i.e. well below 100%) because many users/investors like me don’t mind a small dilution nor want extra risk or complications; and for some others, it’s just impractical to stake for various reasons

Any proposed change to issuance should be based on end-game Ethereum, as the roles of staking participants may get redefined and rewards repriced (maybe proposing can be automated, or mobile validators can stake less ETH, or provers/builders have to stake too)

My vote: do nothing for now

sorry but I don't understand how this is relevant in this context. Can you elaborate your point here? Is the implied conclusion "the current staking level is fine"? If so this is quite far fetched for mainly two reasons: Ethereum is not comparable to the other "coins" in the table and your table shows a snapshot while the issue for Ethereum is the growing trend of more ETH going at stake. As an EU citizen holding euro is a necessity. However rational or irretional you consider the economic actors to be, they face transaction and opportunity costs at all kind of levels. Daily life needs along with "shoeleather cost" are the reasons why despite a positie inflation rate you still observe positive balances on checking accounts and cash in circulation.

text:
1. in theory, but these are in contention. If you can only pick one, which matters more to you? (eth is the most decentralised and secure, or eth has the lowest issuance)? i strongly pick the former over the latter, and think we should as a community. A low issuance PoA network is not massively valuable.

2. disagree, why do we observe almost all operators + decentralised staking going to under + solo staking going -90%? (admittedly its not primarily issuance that's causing this its the second order effects, but my point is that as an ecosystem we're failing not thriving on security under the current issuance, and I contend that cutting the security budget would strictly exacerbate it, no one has put forward data nor a model that argues otherwise, just vibe-arguments that it wouldn't be

much worse than now, or that it would be the lesser evil vs a hypothetical alternative scenario they claim is guaranteed to happen if we don't do it).

3. agree (that we disagree). I would contain growth by making staking more risky (eip 7716). I would improve the withdrawal address gini coefficient by making native staking suck less. I would consider rewarding slashing to take the currently stolen keys out of the woodwork before calamity. I would improve the credibility of our ability to socially slash bad behaviour. No one believes we're going to destroy all of coinbase + binance + kraken's retail staked ether if they freeze a north korean address, unless that's a credible threat, social slashing is not a real threat. The first time we're presented with a choice to socially slash, it won't be cut and dry the right thing to do, it would be extremely unpopular and contentious, and i don't believe we have a strong enough immune response to push through that. (see gnosis + balancer hack as the landmark example). 

I think ultimately we have to pick Ethereum's risk; 2/3 companies controlling Ethereum’s fork choice, but it’s only 25%-40% of all eth. Or X companies controlling fork choice, but it’s >70% of all eth. (I think X has to be a double digit number for Ethereum to survive, but won't put a specific number here. I also don't think we go >70 but i'm giving the risks at either extreme here, not the happy outcomes we each want for our preferred path forward).

and maybe i'll float a 4:
• we agree that we'll need to do something about the centralisation of building + proving blocks, and that issuance is a likely lever to pull to try and keep that system viably decentralised. so a change to issuance to protect decentralisation there could have rough consensus.

messages.text:
My concern is the same it has been since this began:

A reduction in staking APR will hurt decentralized home stakers before it meaningfully reduces centralized staking. The opportunity cost for centralized custodians is near zero and the realized costs of home stakers are substantial. 

Yes, some zealots will run net negative but they will be diluted by the centralized custodians. 

This seems self evident to me with *any* form of targeting that connects issuance with an idealized staking ratio. 

If our goal is to make ETH maximally decentralized and minimally inflationary we should think about ways to mitigate the need for stakers and bonds all together. If our goal is maximum decentralization alone, then we seem to be in a fine place and should perhaps consider a partially enshrined rainbow staking system.

text: There's a scaling argument to the issuance topic that doesn't necessarily have anything to do with the specific goal of preventing a runaway "everyone must stake their Ether" situation as dilution concentrates among fewer holders. Instead, the scaling argument is about keeping the validator count low. Validator count is currently trending down as MAX_EB increases and allows more consolidation

. This is a good thing to see, even as the total amount of Ether staked increases.

One problem is that there are only weak incentives to consolidate. It could be entirely plausible that all of the Ether getting staked ends up as a lot of little 32 Ether validators. The validator count could balloon again. This matters for faster finality proposals;

. I can't imagine that anyone would be fine with actually placing a hard cap on the number of validators, so this leaves economic levers. Issuance reduction is one tool for this. Giving incentives to consolidate is another possible tool.

Issuance reduction can also take many forms. I think there's a stake ratio targeting world where everyone is happy. I don't want to see runaway staking where LSTs become dominant over Ether. This has not happened and the status quo since the Merge has been pretty nice. We could keep the exact same curve we have now up to 40%, 50%, whatever and then trend issuance down after the target.

“1. in theory, but these are in contention. If you can only pick one, which matters more to you? (eth is the most decentralised and secure, or eth has the lowest issuance)? i strongly pick the former over the latter, and think we should as a community. A low issuance PoA network is not massively valuable.”

I obviously agree with Oisin : between eth is the most decentralised and secure, or eth has the lowest issuance I would definitely pick the former. Yet, adding to things that are in contention, how much ETH at stake is too much, is there even a level of deposit size that is too much , many here will disagree on this.

To quote the article shared above from Anders:
“The relationship between the staking deposit size D and Ethereum’s security level is not trivial to characterize. On the one hand, we may focus on the value slashed in an attack. Since one million (M) ETH is worth around 2.2 billion dollars today, the cost of attacking Ethereum using some critical proportion of D (which is currently 29M ETH), becomes very high under the threat of slashing. But a higher deposit size also provides Sybil resistance to more subtle forms of degradation to the consensus mechanism that may not immediately lead to slashing (e.g., short reorgs). Notably, the 14M ETH securing Ethereum at The Merge was found sufficiently secure by the ecosystem at the time, in a way acting as a “revealed preference” under those prevailing circumstances. In any case, there comes a point where the marginal increase in security from adding another validator brings less utility than the utility loss to users. A level of D =33.6M ETH has been used as a reference point of when network conditions (and economics) start to degrade. Drake expanded on his reasons for supporting a target of 30M ETH in a recent AMA. This active area of research is related to the concept of “minimum viable issuance (MVI)”

We are at a pivotal point now. Regarding the initial question from
I think we have enough reasons to

text.text: implement MVI so we make ETH both the most decentralised and secure AND the lowest issuance while NOT putting ourselves at risk of losing both.

text:
Sidenote because the topic of solo stakers and diversity will be coming again: when it comes to the validator sets I’m always tempted to look at it from a contestability stand point. If I have to pick, I’m more favorable of a “not so diverse” validator set at a small deposit size because many ETH can come at stake and defend the neutrality if needed versus a revealed not so diverse validator set at a large deposit size. 


“2. Issuance is already higher than necessary, and growing”

Yes and ETH at stake (deposit size) will continue to just snowball from here.


“3. We disagree on the strategy to contain or lower issuance”

Agree that we disagree but nevertheless I feel that we are rather (slowly) converging on a consensus that now is the right time to act on MVI. Giving every actors the proper time to prepare and adapt.

To Oisin’s point: “No one believes we're going to destroy all of coinbase + binance + kraken's retail staked ether if they freeze a north korean address, unless that's a credible threat, social slashing is not a real threat.”I'm much more worried about the defense of Ethereum credible neutrality and OFAC’s history of weaponisation of financial rails versus North Korea, Russia, Iran but also ICC judges. The latter being much more contentious for EU countries.

text:
We can say with very high confidence for institutional money that it will always favor the lowest risk highest rewards option. Right now the best option is in Staking, it will be in staking forever in the current issuance regime. Not changing the issuance is accepting to skew the validator set towards higher market share for centralized parties.

Regarding the solo stakers the individual rationals are hard to sum up and hard to assess. EthStaker has been the main voice for solo stakers to my knowledge through their annual survey: a meaningful and growing minority of solo stakers (35% in 2025, up from 21% in 2024) actively factor ETH supply inflation into their staking decisions. Many explicitly value ETH-as-money over staking yield. The 'cut issuance kills solo stakers' frame, in particular, is contradicted by the 84% who say they wouldn't even leave for higher LST yields (2026 data is coming, see

).

You may reframe that in favor of MVI: Not changing the issuance is very much killing solo stakers, damaging decentralization, constantly lowering their market share, hurting the value of their principal (the 32ETH) to the profit of staking services that have less consideration over the principal valuation and are mainly driven by the fees extracted from the staking rewards.
Again , on solo stakers, (raise your hand if you are solo staking 🙋‍♂️):
we have Anders article proposing a model for solo stakers, backed with data. It is tedious to read but it argues a lot about the ideal target for the Deposit size of ETH at stake (D). From an economic perspective , neither a D that's too high nor too low is desirable for the health of solo stakers.
  If D is too low, their returns are a chaotic lottery. But if D is too high, their yields are crushed below their estimated fixed costs, and they are economically swallowed by massive institutional staking pools. 
There's a sweet spot for D if you care about Solo Stakers, it's at ~25%  .

In practice this is not happening though - LSTs have lost share and it is flowing to centralized players.

Binance, Kraken, and Coinbase are (at least) the same size as Lido. Add in Bitmine and it's ~ 1/3 of the network. This doesn't even include the institutional stake going to the largest Node Operators. 

This obsession with LSTs seems misplaced when the actual data shows the opposite trend. The snowball isn't rolling toward LSTs - it's rolling toward Coinbase, Binance, Kraken, and User 049Ts. 

Those are the entities that folks should be worried about, and all of the issuance/stake cap proposals that I have seen so far will just entrench them further while most importantly killing all incentive for home stakers to spend time running validators.

messages.text:
Tapering issuance to target a lower staking ratio will certainly reduce the incomes of the big players in staking.

The risk of LSTs supplanting ETH applies even if LSTs are not currently dominant because: 
1. In the long run network effects work in their favour and
2. They don't need to be dominant overall to have a big impact - once 90% of ETH is staked then an LST with 25% would still be much more prevalent than raw ETH.

But the main point is that we should not be building a fragile system which relies on short term effects and market structure to avoid bad outcomes. We should have robust incentives.

messages.text:
Back to the high staking ratio problem:  The messages above give some evidence that scenarios such as 90% Eth staked are not so realistic, although are not a proof.  This brings the question: Are we going to update issuance to solve a problem that might never actually occur?

To move from recycled arguments to something concrete: what's genuinely missing is a clean, rigorous analysis of specific staking ranges and what specific Ethereum properties degrade in each range, with solid thinking of the potential scenarios (dystopian scenarios such as "if 90% Eth staked it would be via a single LST, therefore this LST will replace ETH" not treated as deterministic coz this is just one of the many potential scenarios and has many domino effect assumptions in it).  

If that analysis concludes that beyond some threshold the risks become unacceptable, then given that we don’t even know whether we would even reach that range one day, wouldn’t it be more elegant to keep the current curve as default but define a contingency update that activates automatically only if staking crosses that dangerous threshold? If the problem materializes it gets handled; if it doesn't, nothing changes. Why accept the certain costs of a proactive change to hedge against an uncertain future problem?

Then the discussion would take this into account -  saying: "we are solving the staking ratio problem at the cost of accelerating solo staker exit." 

Coz currently, the “need of change” is advocated as something good for solo stakers, but I doubt there would be a single proposal which would indeed help them, coz I don’t think issuance curve update is a tool to help solo stakers.

messages.text:
should the intention be to just kill Lido , the most effective way would be to enshrine liquid staking in protocol. This is absolutely not the intention. The intention of MVI is to guarantee Ethereum remains long term both secure and sound. Reducing issuance aims at:
improving Ethereum security overall security while preventing the security to degrade from too much staking
adjusting our security budget to our security requirement so that we don’t overpay for security
A healthy debate is going on 1. and we -as a community- will hopefully soon converge to the consensus already formed among EF researchers and to my knowledge among core devs: too much staking is bad Ethereum. 
I think we may already agree that an improvement of the Security and the Soundness (“we are not overpaying for anything”) will have positive consequences in the marketability of ETH and long term relevance of Ethereum. 
Regarding soundness specifically, I don’t particularly buy the argument that “it’s too much of a drag for what it is” summarised this way : “come on, we are just diluting yearly by 0.8% and you suggest 0.5%. If the market can’t deal with that 0.3% delta we have much bigger fish to fry and we should focus on X, Y and Z…”. While this is totally avoiding the security reasons behind the proposal, this is going against our whole history of not overpaying for our security, this is creating negative externalities (some with dire consequences on DeFi attractivity Imho), this is compounding, this is ~$1,000,000,000 in excess at today’s price, and this inevitably leads the question of the dilution threshold, at what point does this become our priority, etc. etc. 
Again, the primary reasons are security and soundness, do note that enshrining Liquid staking would defeat the whole purpose. In my opinion, post MVI, LIDO would be sitting at a much more dominant position from a technical moat perspective and a branding lead perspective.

On solo stakers, we have Anders article proposing a model for solo stakers, backed with data. It is tedious to read but it argues a lot about the ideal target for the Deposit size of ETH at stake (D). From an economic perspective , neither a D that's too high nor too low is desirable for the health of solo stakers.
  If D is too low, their returns are a chaotic lottery. But if D is too high, their yields are crushed below their estimated fixed costs, and they are economically swallowed by massive institutional staking pools. 
There's a sweet spot for D if you care about Solo Stakers, it's at ~25%  .


The current regime is hurting you.

hi! 

I haven't followed discussions super super closely from the start but to me the most important thing is: I want the Ethereum economy to be fueled by  trustless money (ETH), and I wouldn’t want money with additional trust assumptions (with varying degrees e.g., stETH ≠ cbETH) to absorb all ETH. With the current curve we don’t really have ways to stop that scenario from happening, and stake capping sounds like a good solution there

in practice I think the only reason I see it as quite “urgent” is because I think issuance reduction would actually hurt businesses/economies built around yield. So I would want to do stake capping

staked ETH goes beyond a given cap we think is reasonable, specifically so we never have to do any kind of strict issuance reduction

and I wouldn’t really say LSTs are a problem per se, but to me the problem really would be unbounded LST growth absorbing all raw ETH and becoming the de facto “money” for Ethereum. So I'd say I agree it's about reducing intermediaries, or rather making sure that all ETH is not intermediated

about specific curves/concrete proposals it might sound a bit weird but I would be happy with any curve that caps stake, again to me the most important part is about protecting ETH and imo it would be pretty cool if people could at least really behind this

All of the people who have written about this have pointed out that LSTs become problematic in a high staking ratio environment. It's not a secret!

It's also not just about Lido. LSTs offered by any big providers including the exchanges could be problematic if they held a large proportion of the ETH supply - arguably moreso.

That doesn't mean anyone wants to kill LSTs or indeed thinks they can be prevented from playing a role. But if the incentives are set to reach equilibrium at a staking ratio with the majority of ETH stays unstaked, rather than persisting with a curve which incentivises further staking all the way to 100%, then the risks they could pose to Ethereum as a whole are reduced.

1. The ETH supply being intermediated (by whomever) is less desirable then a majority of raw ETH
2. Raw ETH has a much better chance of being a form of money in its own economy versus any staked version, but this will not happen if staking is incentivised out to 100%
3. Credible neutrality is reduced if the entire ETH supply is controlled by a few players. In the long run this will make ETH less valuable and Ethereum less secure.
4. Eventual consolidation of staking providers is much worse at 100% versus 33% as there can be no credible threat of social slashing if they misbehave
5. Excess issuance is a cost for holders of raw ETH
6. Solo stakers get forced out as yield is eaten by dilution because they are taxed on nominal yield (but intermediated staking setups can avoid income tax and pay only CGT)

The foundation of MVI is to provide the maximum welfare to protocol participants. Gonna be a little formal here because I'm just copy-pasting some of my writings on the matter. The blue supply curve in the figure is essentially just a future hypothetical supply curve we might consider plausible. At each deposit size ($D$ ETH), it shows the staking yield ($y$) required for the marginal staker to participate. The area below the supply curve therefore represents the aggregate implied cost of staking, while the area above it (capped by the current yield level) represents staker surplus. The costs reflected in this curve are broad: hardware and operating costs, loss of liquidity and other opportunity costs, slashing and counterparty risk, taxes, etc.

The current reward curve in black compels users to incur higher costs than necessary for securing Ethereum. Reducing issuance to a new reward curve in orange improves welfare by lowering these costs in aggregate (not claiming here that this specific curve is ideal).

messages.text:
The light blue area removed by the equilibrium shift is the key welfare gain. It represents costs that the protocol no longer induces ETH holders to incur. Under the higher-issuance equilibrium, additional ETH is staked only because the protocol pays enough to compensate users for those extra costs. Under the lower-issuance equilibrium, that compensation is no longer paid, leading stakers to withdraw stake such that these costs no longer need to be incurred.

Excessive issuance pressures holders into an artificial choice: either remain non-stakers and accept dilution, or stake in order to offset that dilution while incurring the costs and risks of staking. One example of such risks would be the recent KelpUser 049O exploit. We want users to be able to hold the ETH token while attaining the maximum welfare, and thus we want to reduce issuance.

This is a trick question. 😅 I've read your articles on this, know the total size of LRT/LST market irrespective of chain (~80B) & ETH supply which is staked (% market share for sector concentrated among few players like LIDO ~47% ) and research reports that predict YOY growth rate of the sector by 2030-2035.

Solana is having their own debate that they'll hit stake centralization & consolidation within the next 2-3 yrs.

And yet - I think that Ethereum has more time at its disposal to address this issue & study the effects of how it impacts other chains first.

Tinkering with incentives makes the assumption all economic actors in the market are rational, and using it as a disincentivization tool will stop them from vying for more network control (which isn't necessarily true).

One question I do want to ask is : How do we determine that high staking ratio above X% is what threatens the security of Ethereum? 

In what way 
- preventing double spends?
- or X% of single LST operator supply/total LST supply, Y% locked in Defi can act as structural threat to the demand, safety and censorship resistance of Ethereum.
- raw ETH ownership proportional to total stablecoin/RWA's deployed by an asset issuer.

As of now - none of the articles I've read adequately define what a "security" framework is in this context.

OUser 079 - no one wants double spend attacks to happen, or LUNA style contagion effect to ravage Ethereum, or few actor collectives, or in isolation influencing the fork choice -  but I feel the proposal is a bit premature & few bips of public welfare/choking LST yield for larger institutional players still doesn't help me.

I’d like to offer some pushback. As always I appreciate you and the RIGs thorough feedback on this topic. 

I agree that there are more worlds with a positive real yield in the low issuance environment. However, my concern is that this analysis is conflating two separate decisions and ascribing the same logical decision structure to both. 

First there is the question of whether one wants to hold or not hold ETH. I fully grant that the lower issuance world is better for this. However, there is a tangential question of whether one wants to stake or not. 

The incentives around the latter point are more important for determining the quality of stake than the former. The large majority of the benefits from the lower issuance world are had by all ETH holders, which sounds nice, but removes onus for people to want to stake. 

This is where nominal yield becomes a factor. If the real yield is positive 1.5% but 1.3% of that is coming from the burn and supply contraction, then the nominal yield offers a weak incentive for people to move from holders to stakers. 

How do you maintain the quality of stake in this world?

Your framing is I think one of the clearest in this debate. So, let me ask, what the "given cap we think is reasonable" is and how far are we from it, if it ever happens, this is my main misunderstanding here. This is also what should define the urgency and the approach I believe. 

If the problem is "not 100% ETH staked", then would disallowing more than e.g., 70% work? Since we don't know even whether this would be reached with current curve, instead of speculating "this would happen" / "this would not happen" like kids, wouldn't it make sense to keep the current curve and introduce a different behavior in case that 70% is reached, if that ever happens? Would that solve the issue? 

Same question might be applicable for LST percentage. What % ETH being in a single LST is considered bad? Currently ~33% ETH is staked and no LST has more than 25%, meaning 8.3% of total ETH. What is the threshold that a single LST becomes a potential replacement of ETH and how many years far away is it? 

I am asking, coz I feel that there is no real urgency and that stake capping you are suggesting can be applied without changing the curve in the "reasonable" eth staked regimes. At least this is my understanding on how the problem you pose could be approached.

text:
I tried to sum this up in this following few liners, I may have forgotten or simplified the model so let me know if you spot something wrong.

Let’s sum up the “control” thresholds. The bottom line is that above 50%, we need to have fresher ETH coming at staking to resume normal operation.
At pretty low threshold, you may start delaying finality for MEV exploits or messing with services that rely on block finality like bridges and CEX deposit, L2 settlement etc. Our defense mechanism is inactivity Leak but also fresh honest ETH coming at stake.

text.text: What can you do if you have X% of the ETH at stake?

text:
With a lot of effort, you may delay -for a little while- the consensus finality but you’ll burn your ETH doing so. Execution continues.
=> small finality delay, more mischief will set your ETH on fire

With some effort, you can delay -for a little while- the consensus finality but you’ll burn your ETH doing so. Execution continues.
=> medium finality delay, more mischief will set your ETH on fire

With little effort, you can do short reorgs, censor transactions, maximize MEV for yourself etc. 
Only through social coordination, new (honest) ETH need to come at stake to lower your grip while honest validators create a minority fork burning your ETH in the process. Execution continues, potentially with censorship and short term uncertainty on the history.
=> finality delay, double finality, censorship, control over blockchain future

Same as above but major social coordination is required to take over the chain (and burn your ETH in the process) and Execution has long term uncertainty.
=> same as above with control over blockchain future AND past

messages.text: If there is one specific target stake, then the issuance, inflation and nominal  yield can in theory go from negative infinity to positive infinity. If there is one target issuance/inflation rate, then stake participation can go from 0 to the entire supply. For this reason, reward curves tend to be these types of downward-sloping shapes you have seen in various figures, to parry the extremes. To get a number, you need to combine a hypothesis of the shape of the supply curve, with an equation for the reward curve, and calculate it at the equilibrium.

Apologies for the delay - med school and what not. I don’t find the FAQ compelling on all points though overall it is very well written. I will list out the specific areas of modeling I think need exploration. I do appreciate that a large chunk of the FAQ is dedicated to stake set quality. 

First, the paragraph describing a drop off yield value makes no attempt to model costs that would inform the decisions leading to the drop off. VB’s suggesting 0.8% yearly costs seems pertinent here. 

Second, dominate SSP advantage. I disagree with the characterization that the competitive advantage of economies of scale is more obvious at higher quantities of ETH staked. If we take the extreme end of the current curve, the difference in yields between solo staking and LSTs in an absolute sense is small. However, at lower ratios the absolute advantage is larger — eg, a 0 fee custodial CEX will have a considerately higher yield than solo staking. A reasonable rebuttal is that we adjust overall issuance down so that we get the same absolute differential but at lower ratios. However, the absolute advantage persists, just at a different spot on the curve. 

I agree with the arguments about moneyness and social overloading. 

I do not believe we will ever be in a paradigm where the risks of delegating are significant enough to create a large enough risk premium that people move towards solo staking. I agree that lower yield will lead to lower *staking demand* but not relatively more solo staking demand. We already see people sticking their ETH into CB for higher relative risk and lower relative yield. Importantly, it’s hard to imagine a world where the relative risks of delegating vs holding ETH vs solo staking are substantially different over long time frames. 

Next, negative yield and altruism. I think this section has a glaring missing piece which is that staked Eth can/already is offered as a loss leader to become the platform of a person’s assets. This isn’t monopolizing a key function of Ethereum or any nefarious attack. I think it’s reasonable to believe that companies are more willing to burn some cash to get people’s business than people are willing to lose money on their own staking set up. This is especially true if restaking naked ETH is an option to them. I take issue with the suggest intercepts at 0 yield in figure 10. 

The supply of home stakers. I believe this section mistakes the cap on available solo stakers with a cap on solo staked ETH. ETH delegated to home stakers is the current best defense of Ethereum neutrality / staking capture. The amount of ETH provided by node operators can be matched at a decently high multiple and still offer sufficient “skin in the game” - I believe Dankrad wrote a good article on this some years ago. 

Finally I want to say I support a thoughtful change to staking and think there is a path forward - I just don’t see that path involving a cap unless it’s after rainbow staking and similar stratify out responsibilities and we can depend less on home stakers. I largely agree with the final paragraph of the endgame policy. I support some degree of tempering but not a capping mechanism prior to other protective measures being implemented. The issue here is perceptions.

However, at lower ratios the absolute advantage is larger — eg, a 0 fee custodial CEX will have a considerately higher yield than solo staking. A reasonable rebuttal is that we adjust overall issuance down so that we get the same absolute differential but at lower ratios. However, the absolute advantage persists, just at a different spot on the curve. 

I agree with the arguments about moneyness and social overloading. 

I do not believe we will ever be in a paradigm where the risks of delegating are significant enough to create a large enough risk premium that people move towards solo staking. I agree that lower yield will lead to lower *staking demand* but not relatively more solo staking demand. We already see people sticking their ETH into CB for higher relative risk and lower relative yield. Importantly, it’s hard to imagine a world where the relative risks of delegating vs holding ETH vs solo staking are substantially different over long time frames. 

Next, negative yield and altruism. I think this section has a glaring missing piece which is that staked Eth can/already is offered as a loss leader to become the platform of a person’s assets. This isn’t monopolizing a key function of Ethereum or any nefarious attack. I think it’s reasonable to believe that companies are more willing to burn some cash to get people’s business than people are willing to lose money on their own staking set up. This is especially true if restaking naked ETH is an option to them. I take issue with the suggest intercepts at 0 yield in figure 10. 

The supply of home stakers. I believe this section mistakes the cap on available solo stakers with a cap on solo staked ETH. ETH delegated to home stakers is the current best defense of Ethereum neutrality / staking capture. The amount of ETH provided by node operators can be matched at a decently high multiple and still offer sufficient “skin in the game” - I believe Dankrad wrote a good article on this some years ago. 

Finally I want to say I support a thoughtful change to staking and think there is a path forward - I just don’t see that path involving a cap unless it’s after rainbow staking and similar stratify out responsibilities and we can depend less on home stakers. I largely agree with the final paragraph of the endgame policy. I support some degree of tempering but not a capping mechanism prior to other protective measures being implemented. The issue here is perceptions.

messages.text:
indeed the issuance has a "net issuance" cousin (newly minted ETH rewarded to active validators minus burnt ETH from activities related to EIP 1559 & 4844).

Couple of context remarks:

- 1559 burn arises from spikes in activity 
- 4844 burn arises from blob consumption

We experienced a regime in the past for about 18 months, from ~Sep 2022  (Post Merge, no more issuance from PoW)  till ~March 2024 (EIP 4844 introduces blobs), where the net issuance was rather negative. The Ultrasound money narrative was a powerful one but unfortunately short lived. Ethereum couldn't stay Ultrasound and scale (as in -keep blockspace affordable-). This period was very painful for L2s who had to keep posting their history on the L1, creating a constant demand from blockspace, keeping average gas price and utilisation rate of block high. Consequently any small spike in activity triggered massive burn of ETH while preventing small holders from transacting. L2s were not even competitive in this period because they had to pass the extra cost in gas to their users and were barely able to propose a x3 to a x6 reduction in transaction cost for their users.
Competition was coming at Ethereum through a new wave of alt L1 Ethereum killers or suggesting short term storage solutions to the L2s leveraging the validator sets (restaking eigenlayer and others).
It was not a great time to be an Ethereum user.

EIP 4844 was long awaited and changed the paradigm totally for L2s. The idea that Ethereum is too expensive rapidly disappeared and opponents shifted the narrative to Ethereum is slow or L2s are not Ethereum. 
EIP 4844 was shipped with a wrongly calibrated blob market which took arguably too long to fix (via EIP 7918 last December). The blob price was stuck at its minimum and is now  behaving much more correctly. What Ethereum got is L2 Affordability as well as a great defense against of other L1s and against restaking value capture.

Some may argue that a few L2s (wink Base?) are value extracting from Ethereum because they dont pay that much in sequencing fees compared to what they pocket when charging their users. I say it's fair enough and good for them, at the end of day they are giving a 0x to many new comers. Appchain are now kicking in, Lighter is doing 1000 Tps on a 24h averable, we must be happy to have that on Ethereum albeit through a L2 compared to sending this activity to Hyperliquid. 

I am personally a strong believer in L2-fication. Alt L1s have tk realise they would be better off not over spending for their security with badly designed PoS and sequence in Ethereum instead. Celo is a great example,  Ronin is another one just announced. 
The L2s and hopefully other use cases for blobs are a great source of burn and thus reduction of the net issuance. All the money spent on blob is burnt.

1559 burn is coming from spikes in usage which( mostly if not always ) nowadays come from considerable ETH price movement. The transaction pipeline industry (the block builders) are mostly supportive of issuance reduction for the reason that they expect it to catalize the DeFi activity and thus MEV and likely the burn as well.

By no means are we introducing a Minimum Viable Issuance to the community without considering the burn. It is nevertheless a second order effect, hard to estimate but a positive externality for every holders staking or not.

Let's look at the situation we are in right now:

Ethereum is in a critical adoption phase, we are:
- Relentlessly progressing on its missing interoperability features 
- Scaling the L1
- Catching up on compulsory privacy features for institutional adoption
- Sponsoring L2 at the cost of our fees with cheap blobs
- Relentlessly keeping up with attractiveness for potential new adoption waves of adoption (say AI Agents, predictive markets etc.)
- Gearing up for the next wave of ETH killers.

messages.text:
Reasonable point. Coinbase is a bigger risk today than any other single source of concentration, for sure. But that just hammers home one of the concerns here.

Roughly a third of ETH is staked today. If we are talking about 50-70% of all ETH being staked, and the largest institutional/custodial providers merely retain market share, then we start recreating a 2008-style too-big-to-fail dynamic inside Ethereum.

There are multiple reasons to address issuance/staking economics, and they are not mutually exclusive. Dilution, concentration, exit queue dynamics, moral hazard, and the risk of ETH losing its role as the dominant trustless collateral are all interlinked by network effects and economic incentives.

The deeper issue is that if the liquid collateral layer migrates from ETH to governed or custodial claims on ETH, Ethereum becomes less credibly neutral. Native ETH is the trustless base asset; wrappers reintroduce governance, custody, smart-contract, and operator risk.

If we do not address this soon, Ethereum risks creating at least one, and perhaps multiple, entities that are effectively too big to fail.

messages.text:
Countless research posts discuss several arguments for a new reward curve that reduces issuance. If you feel that one argument is stronger than the other, that is fine. If you feel that one argument is not relevant, it is better to address it to make the case for why it is not relevant. 

As an example of an argument you seem to not find relevant: The current reward curve compels users to incur higher costs than necessary for securing Ethereum (costs broadly defined to include hardware, risks, illiquidity, taxes, etc.). Reducing issuance improves welfare by lowering these costs in aggregate. This is of course strongly related to the issuance rate, under any reasonable shape of the stake supply curve.

And look how that turned out to be. The effect of burn wasn't sufficient enough against nominal inflation during reflexive market downturn as activity scaled down w decreasing fees, L2's inadvertently drew activity away from the L1 while providing lesser security guarantees & paid lesser fees.

Blockspace premium that was thought to exist and persist evaporated, digital oil theorists were all wrong for confusing a pocket of onchain economy flourishing as onchain economy doing well & improving - volatility has been abundant, but ETH has been underperforming against its USD valuation pair, thanks to little bit of financial engineering from our free market friends,

It's time to take non-security interests & ecosystem demand into factor as well when security/nominal yield related discussions are considered if EF is to pursue alternative store of value thesis ahead.

They can't be cast aside as non-essential parameters.

Pre-21' - most of Ethereum's accelerated demand was catalysed in terms of priority fees paid because of NFT szn (full blown market mania). Deflationary burn was seen as a positive during this low interest rate environment with upward reflexivity.

Yes - EIP 1559 made the network more accessible & fixed broken fee market, but base fee burn also impacted miner profitability to an extent (& these were ppl like solo stakers who used to hold ETH for much longer even during times of market distress - similar to BTC miners). 

In an interest rate constrained environment - a lot of onchain activity simply cratered and never reached previous highs in terms of net fees accumulated by the network. 

With blobs announcement, you can see on

that the issuance since around that time has been uponly.

In short, my view is that any changes to monetary policy should also take a credible, opinonated view on how it affects the onchain economy (Defi..) and how it can stakeholder ownership behavior too.

messages.text:
TradFi analysts still view the sector as low-margin high volume SaaS, a momentum asset w high volatility.
ETH for better or worse is corr to BTC, while being in direct conflict w its artificial scarcity proposition - which takes view that consistent fiat debasement from all centrally planned economies eats into consumer savings & purchasing power. So let's be very careful we are not reinventing a slightly worse version of an existing financial system onchain.

The market is a game of poker bw sophisticated & uniformed flow - even TradFi User 049T buyers that have purchased this raw ETH that they'll stake as centralised actors will have a view if Eth economy is flourishing or not, how interest rate cuts to LST's will affect the nominal yield they provide to their investors, if they're able to maintain > 1 NAV w enough cash in hand & weather downturn/suppression & not become forced sellers.

So, the key to good policy design is factoring in human behavior to prevent outcomes that push into downward reflexive spirals.
